Thanks. Here's the provisional **Creative Brief**, built from what you've told me so far:

> You want a long-haul, slow-burn survival game that blends **Challenge & Mastery** with **Story & Discovery**. Players should feel pressure from the systems and also feel the dread of slowly learning what the web is. Your touchstones are the cosmic trap of *Aquila Rift*, the waking-into-wrongness of *Pandorum*, and the base-and-scavenge long tail of *Project Zomboid*. There's no deadline, and this is your first game, which matters a lot for how we scope it. We'll treat "no end game beyond survival" as a design strength, not a license for unlimited features.

I haven't had your answers to the two typed questions yet, and they shape the concepts I'll propose:

1. A game moment that genuinely thrilled, scared, or absorbed you, and what created it.
2. Your 3 most-played games, and what kept you coming back.

Answer those (a sentence each is plenty) and correct anything in the brief that's off. Then I'll generate three distinct concept directions for you to react to.
1) building a base with friends in project zomboid that becomes self sufficient and survivable.  2) project zomboid, satisfactory, stellaris

That's a clear signal. Your anchor moment is **cooperative self-sufficiency**: a base that goes from fragile to survivable, built *with* people. Zomboid gives you the slow systemic survival, Satisfactory the joy of a logistics machine that hums, Stellaris the pleasure of a galaxy that slowly reveals its horrors. The podcraft-and-weld idea is really "Satisfactory's factory meets Zomboid's safehouse, in Aquila Rift's web."

Updated brief in one line: *a cooperative, long-tail survival sim where the base is a ship you assemble from the wreckage of others, and the deeper you go the less sane you are.*

Here are three concept directions. They all keep your seed, but each puts a different thing at the center.

---

### Concept 1 — **Salvage Fleet**
*(Verb-first: BUILD)*

- **Elevator Pitch**: Wake in a dead ship's cryo bay. Patch a podcraft, fly to neighbouring derelicts, and weld their halves into a growing home-ship. Then push toward the center of the web, where the horrors and the best hulls are.
- **Core Verb**: Weld (reclaim a part, bring it home, join it on).
- **Core Fantasy**: "We built this from corpses of ships, and it flies."
- **Unique Hook**: Like Project Zomboid's safehouse, AND ALSO your base is modular, mobile, and made of other ships.
- **Primary MDA Aesthetic**: Expression (with Challenge second).
- **Scope**: Large.
- **Why It Could Work**: Ship-building is a proven magnet (Space Engineers, Starbound, Cosmoteer), and no one has put it inside a cosmic-horror survival sim.
- **Biggest Risk**: Modular 2D ship assembly with working life-support, hull integrity, and multiplayer sync is the hardest technical problem on the list, and it's the one everything else sits on.

---

### Concept 2 — **The Long Dark Between**
*(Experience-first: DREAD via DISCOVERY)*

- **Elevator Pitch**: You and your crew don't know how long you've been asleep, where you are, or why the ship's logs stop. Survival is the backdrop; the game is piecing together the web's story from every derelict you board, while the web pieces *you* apart.
- **Core Verb**: Investigate (board, read, record, flee).
- **Core Fantasy**: "We're the only ones awake, and we're starting to understand what that means."
- **Unique Hook**: Like Zomboid's survival, AND ALSO the sanity system is a narrative instrument. Hallucinations lie to you, and you can't always tell whose logs are real.
- **Primary MDA Aesthetic**: Narrative / Discovery.
- **Scope**: Large.
- **Why It Could Work**: *Aquila Rift* and *Pandorum* fans are an under-served audience; story-rich co-op survival (*Barotrauma*, *Lethal Company*) shows the appetite.
- **Biggest Risk**: Authored mystery and procedurally generated derelicts pull against each other. The story needs enough hand-placed content to pay off, and that's expensive for a solo first-timer.

---

### Concept 3 — **Hull Pressure**
*(Mashup: survival sim + logistics machine)*

- **Elevator Pitch**: Every ship in the web is a leaking system. Oxygen, heat, power and sanity all drain, and the only way to stop the drain is to build chains of salvaged machinery that feed each other. Flying toward the center means more inputs, more outputs, and more that can go wrong at once.
- **Core Verb**: Balance (route, repair, re-route).
- **Core Fantasy**: "The ship is alive because we keep it alive, minute by minute."
- **Unique Hook**: Like Satisfactory's production chains, AND ALSO the whole factory is a life-support system under eldritch attack.
- **Primary MDA Aesthetic**: Challenge (systems mastery).
- **Scope**: Medium–Large.
- **Why It Could Work**: Oxygen Not Included and Satisfactory prove the systems-balancing crowd is huge and patient; horror adds a hook they haven't had.
- **Biggest Risk**: Deep resource simulation can swallow the horror. If players stare at pipes all night, the dread never lands.

---

I'd note the obvious: your real game is probably a blend, with 1 as the spine. But see which one *pulls*.

# Director Gates — Shared Review Pattern

Index of all director and lead review gates. Skills reference gate IDs from this
index instead of embedding prompts inline — eliminating drift when prompts need
updating. Each gate's full definition (Trigger, Context to pass, Prompt, Verdicts)
lives in its own file under `.claude/docs/director-gates/`, named after the gate
ID in lowercase.

**Scope**: All 7 production stages (Concept → Release), all 3 Tier 1 directors,
all key Tier 2 leads. Any skill, team orchestrator, or workflow may invoke these gates.

**When a skill spawns a director for a gate, it must NOT read the gate definition
file itself. Include the gate definition file path in the `Agent` prompt and instruct
the director agent to read it first, then pass only the context fields that gate's
row requires. Gate definitions are read by the spawned agent, in the agent's own
context window.**

---

## Gate Index

Agent by prefix: `CD-` creative-director · `TD-` technical-director ·
`PR-` producer · `AD-` art-director · `LP-` lead-programmer · `QL-` qa-lead ·
`ND-` narrative-director. Definition files below are in
`.claude/docs/director-gates/`; each one's header names its agent's model tier.

| Gate ID | Purpose | Definition file |
|---------|---------|-----------------|
| CD-PILLARS | Pillar stress test after pillars are defined | cd-pillars.md |
| CD-GDD-ALIGN | GDD pillar alignment after a system GDD is authored | cd-gdd-align.md |
| CD-SYSTEMS | Systems decomposition vision check after `/map-systems` | cd-systems.md |
| CD-NARRATIVE | Narrative consistency of story/lore documents | cd-narrative.md |
| CD-PLAYTEST | Player experience validation of playtest reports | cd-playtest.md |
| CD-PHASE-GATE | Creative readiness at phase transition | cd-phase-gate.md |
| TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY | System boundary review before GDD authoring | td-system-boundary.md |
| TD-FEASIBILITY | Technical feasibility of early concept risks | td-feasibility.md |
| TD-ARCHITECTURE | Master architecture document sign-off | td-architecture.md |
| TD-ADR | Individual ADR review before Accepted | td-adr.md |
| TD-ENGINE-RISK | Engine version risk for post-cutoff APIs | td-engine-risk.md |
| TD-PHASE-GATE | Technical readiness at phase transition | td-phase-gate.md |
| TD-MANIFEST | Control manifest review before it is written | td-manifest.md |
| TD-CHANGE-IMPACT | Design-change impact assessment review | td-change-impact.md |
| PR-SCOPE | Scope and timeline validation | pr-scope.md |
| PR-SPRINT | Sprint plan feasibility review | pr-sprint.md |
| PR-MILESTONE | Milestone risk assessment | pr-milestone.md |
| PR-EPIC | Epic structure feasibility before story breakdown | pr-epic.md |
| PR-PHASE-GATE | Production readiness at phase transition | pr-phase-gate.md |
| AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL | Visual identity anchor after pillars lock | ad-concept-visual.md |
| AD-ART-BIBLE | Art bible sign-off before asset production | ad-art-bible.md |
| AD-PHASE-GATE | Visual readiness at phase transition | ad-phase-gate.md |
| LP-FEASIBILITY | Implementation feasibility of the architecture | lp-feasibility.md |
| LP-CODE-REVIEW | Code review of an implemented story | lp-code-review.md |
| QL-STORY-READY | Acceptance-criteria testability before sprint | ql-story-ready.md |
| QL-TEST-COVERAGE | Test coverage review for one story before it closes (`/story-done`) | ql-test-coverage.md |
| ND-CONSISTENCY | Narrative consistency of writer deliverables | nd-consistency.md |
| AD-VISUAL | Visual consistency of art/tech-art decisions | ad-visual.md |

---

## Review Modes

Review intensity controls whether gates run.

**Global config**: `modes.review_mode` in `project.yaml` — one word: `full`,
`lean`, or `solo`. Legacy fallback: `production/review-mode.txt` (single line,
same values); `project.yaml` wins when both are present. `/start` never writes
it: left unset, it follows `modes.rigor` (`minimal` → `solo`, `standard` →
`lean`, `full` → `full`). Set it explicitly only with
`/settings modes.review_mode=<value>`.

**Per-run override**: any gate-using skill accepts `--review [full|lean|solo]`,
overriding the global config for that run only.

| Mode | What runs |
|------|-----------|
| `full` | All gates active — every workflow step reviewed |
| `lean` | PHASE-GATEs only (`/gate-check`) — per-skill gates skipped. The `rigor: standard` value |
| `solo` | No director gates anywhere (game jams, prototypes, max speed). **Default** — the `rigor: minimal` value |

**One exception:** `/team-narrative` runs ND-CONSISTENCY in every review mode
whenever narrative-director is on the team — it is that pipeline's only
narrative consistency check, not an optional review.

---

## Invocation Pattern (copy into any skill)

**MANDATORY: apply the review mode before every gate spawn.**

The value is already resolved — skills call
`` !`bash "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../../hooks/yaml-helper.sh" resolve_config --keys review_mode` ``
(with the matching `allowed-tools` grant — see `config-resolution.md`)
and read `review_mode` from the emitted block. Do **not** re-derive it here. The
full chain (`project.local.yaml` → `project.yaml` → `production/review-mode.txt`
→ `modes.rigor` expansion, `standard`→`lean`), its defaults and its failure modes are specified in
`.claude/docs/config-resolution.md`, and covered by the config test suite.

An inline `--review [mode]` argument, if the skill accepts one, overrides the
resolved value for that run.

Apply the resolved mode:
- `solo` → **skip all gates**. Note: `[GATE-ID] skipped — Solo mode`
- `lean` → **skip unless this is a PHASE-GATE** (CD-PHASE-GATE, TD-PHASE-GATE, PR-PHASE-GATE, AD-PHASE-GATE). Note: `[GATE-ID] skipped — Lean mode`
- `full` → spawn as normal

> **PHASE-GATE panel width is a second, independent axis.** `review_mode` decides
> whether the four PHASE-GATEs run at all; `modes.workflow` decides how many of
> them run — `minimal` → PR only, `standard` → TD + PR, `full` → all four. The
> rule and its rationale live in `/gate-check` Section 4b, the only skill that
> spawns PHASE-GATEs. Every other gate in this index is single-director and
> unaffected. Width never softens a verdict: the escalation rule below applies
> unchanged to whoever ran.

```
# Apply mode check, then:
Spawn `[agent-name]` via `Agent`:
- Gate: [GATE-ID] — `Agent` prompt instructs the agent to read
  `.claude/docs/director-gates/[gate-id].md` FIRST (parent must not read it)
- Context: [fields under that gate's **Context to pass**]
- Await the verdict before proceeding.
```

For parallel spawning (multiple directors at one gate point): apply the mode
check per gate, then spawn all surviving agents simultaneously — issue all `Agent`
calls before waiting for any result; collect all verdicts before proceeding.

---

## Standard Verdict Format

Every gate returns one of its three verdicts — or NOT ASSESSED when it could not
judge. Skills must handle all four. The three judgement words are each gate's
own — its definition file's **Verdicts** line is the authority — and the rows
below are their meanings (TD-FEASIBILITY's VIABLE / CONCERNS / HIGH RISK,
PR-MILESTONE's ON TRACK / AT RISK / OFF TRACK). NOT ASSESSED is the same word at
every gate, so no Verdicts line lists it:

| Verdict | Meaning | Default action |
|---------|---------|----------------|
| **APPROVE / READY** | No issues. Proceed. | Continue the workflow |
| **CONCERNS [list]** | Issues present but not blocking. | Surface to user via `AskUserQuestion` — options: `Revise flagged items` / `Accept and proceed` / `Discuss further`. Revise flagged items: the specialist who drafted the section re-drafts it; the revision goes through the skill's normal approve-then-write step, and the header records `REVISED [date]`. |
| **REJECT / NOT READY [blockers]** | Blocking issues. Do not proceed. | Surface blockers to user. Do not write files or advance stage until resolved. |
| **NOT ASSESSED [what was missing]** | An input the gate names was missing or unreadable, so no judgement was made. | Name what was missing. Never treat it as APPROVE/READY: supply the input and re-run the gate, or record NOT ASSESSED and let the skill's own verdict reflect it. |

**Rank**: NOT ASSESSED sits below REJECT / NOT READY and CONCERNS, and above
APPROVE / READY — a known problem is more actionable than an unknown, and a gate
that could not look has approved nothing. A director that found a problem and
also lacked an input answers with the problem's word and names the missing
input in its rationale. An artifact the skill reports as absent is information,
not a missing input. At a phase gate,
a missing artifact the target phase requires is a finding (NOT READY or
CONCERNS); one `/gate-check` passes as "not expected before [phase]" or "not
required at `workflow: [tier]`" is not a finding — a phase gate judges
readiness for the phase being entered, not a later one.

**Escalation rule**: When multiple directors are spawned in parallel, apply the
strictest verdict by that rank — one NOT READY overrides all READY verdicts, and
one NOT ASSESSED keeps the result from being READY.

---

## Recording Gate Outcomes

After a gate resolves, record the verdict in the relevant document's status header:

```markdown
> **[Director] Review ([GATE-ID])**: APPROVED [date] / CONCERNS (accepted) [date] / REVISED [date] / NOT ASSESSED [date] — [missing input]
```

For phase gates, record in `docs/architecture/architecture.md` or
`production/session-state/active.md` as appropriate.

---

## Parallel Gate Protocol

At checkpoints needing multiple directors (most common at `/gate-check`):

```
Spawn in parallel (issue all `Agent` calls before waiting for any result):
creative-director → CD-PHASE-GATE, technical-director → TD-PHASE-GATE,
producer → PR-PHASE-GATE, art-director → AD-PHASE-GATE

Collect every verdict from the directors that ran, then apply escalation rules:
- Any NOT READY / REJECT → overall verdict minimum FAIL
- Any CONCERNS → overall verdict minimum CONCERNS
- Any NOT ASSESSED (and no NOT READY / REJECT or CONCERNS) → overall verdict at best NOT ASSESSED
- All READY / APPROVE → eligible for PASS (still subject to artifact checks)
```

---

## Gate Coverage by Stage

| Stage | Required Gates | Optional Gates |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Concept** | CD-PILLARS, AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL | TD-FEASIBILITY, PR-SCOPE |
| **Systems Design** | TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY, CD-SYSTEMS, PR-SCOPE, CD-GDD-ALIGN (per GDD) | ND-CONSISTENCY, AD-VISUAL, TD-CHANGE-IMPACT (on GDD revision) |
| **Technical Setup** | TD-ARCHITECTURE, TD-ADR (per ADR), TD-MANIFEST, LP-FEASIBILITY, AD-ART-BIBLE | TD-ENGINE-RISK |
| **Pre-Production** | PR-EPIC, QL-STORY-READY (per story), PR-SPRINT, the PHASE-GATE panel (via gate-check — PR at `minimal`, TD + PR at `standard`, all four at `full`) | CD-PLAYTEST |
| **Production** | LP-CODE-REVIEW (per story), QL-STORY-READY, PR-SPRINT (per sprint), QL-TEST-COVERAGE (per story, via `/story-done`) | PR-MILESTONE, AD-VISUAL, TD-CHANGE-IMPACT (on GDD revision) |
| **Polish** | CD-PLAYTEST, PR-MILESTONE | AD-VISUAL |
| **Release** | The PHASE-GATE panel (via gate-check — PR at `minimal`, TD + PR at `standard`, all four at `full`) | — |

# Game Concept: [Working Title]

*Created: [Date]*
*Status: [Draft / Under Review / Approved]*

---

## Elevator Pitch

> [1-2 sentences that capture the entire game. Should be compelling enough to
> make someone want to hear more. Format: "It's a [genre] where you [core
> action] in a [setting] to [goal]."
>
> Test: Can someone who has never heard of this game understand what they'd
> be doing in 10 seconds? If not, simplify.]

---

## Core Identity

| Aspect | Detail |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Genre** | [Primary genre + subgenre(s)] |
| **Platform** | [PC / Console / Mobile / Cross-platform] |
| **Target Audience** | [See Player Profile section below] |
| **Player Count** | [Single-player / Co-op / Multiplayer / MMO] |
| **Session Length** | [Typical play session: 10 min / 30 min / 1 hr / 2+ hr] |
| **Monetization** | [Premium / F2P / Subscription / none yet] |
| **Estimated Scope** | [Small (1-3 months) / Medium (3-9 months) / Large (9+ months)] |
| **Comparable Titles** | [2-3 existing games in the same space] |

---

## Core Fantasy

[What power, experience, or feeling does the player get from this game?
What can they do here that they can't do anywhere else?

The core fantasy is the emotional promise. It's not a feature list — it's the
answer to "why would someone choose THIS game over anything else they could
be doing?"

Examples of strong core fantasies:
- "You are a lone survivor building a new life in a hostile wilderness" (survival)
- "You command a civilization across millennia" (strategy)
- "You explore a vast, beautiful world at your own pace" (open world)
- "You master intricate combat and overcome impossible odds" (soulslike)]

---

## Unique Hook

[What makes this game different from everything else in its genre? This is
the single most important differentiator.

A strong hook passes the "and also" test: "It's like [comparable game],
AND ALSO [unique thing]." If the "and also" doesn't spark curiosity, the
hook needs work.

The hook should be:
- Explainable in one sentence
- Genuinely novel (not just a combination of existing features)
- Connected to the core fantasy (not a gimmick bolted on)
- Something that affects gameplay, not just aesthetics]

---

## Player Experience Analysis (MDA Framework)

The MDA (Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics) framework ensures we design from the
player's emotional experience backward to the systems that create it.

### Target Aesthetics (What the player FEELS)
Rank the following aesthetic goals for this game (1 = primary, mark N/A if not
relevant). These come from the MDA framework's 8 aesthetic categories:

| Aesthetic | Priority | How We Deliver It |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Sensation** (sensory pleasure) | [1-8 or N/A] | [Visual beauty, audio design, haptics] |
| **Fantasy** (make-believe, role-playing) | [Priority] | [World, characters, player identity] |
| **Narrative** (drama, story arc) | [Priority] | [Plot structure, player-driven stories] |
| **Challenge** (obstacle course, mastery) | [Priority] | [Difficulty curve, skill ceiling] |
| **Fellowship** (social connection) | [Priority] | [Co-op, guilds, shared experiences] |
| **Discovery** (exploration, secrets) | [Priority] | [Hidden areas, emergent systems, lore] |
| **Expression** (self-expression, creativity) | [Priority] | [Build variety, cosmetics, creation tools] |

content.text:
Both answers feed straight into the design. "Deliberate *and* frantic" isn't a contradiction, it's a **two-rhythm loop**: the slow, listening dread of boarding, and the chaos when the web turns its head. "The web notices you" is the mechanism that flips one into the other. I'm drafting the loops and pillars below, then (per `autonomous`) locking the pillars and sending them to the directors in parallel.

---

## Core Loop

**30-second (two rhythms)**
- *Boarding rhythm* — cut a hatch, listen, sweep a light, read a dead ship's gauges, decide whether a part is worth the noise of taking it. Zomboid-paced; every door is a decision.
- *Breach rhythm* — the web has noticed: a hull section fails, power drops, something wakes. Patch, re-route, retreat to the pod. Barotrauma-paced.
- *The hinge*: an **Attention** state. Light, noise, power spikes, and depth in the web raise it. Boarding becomes breach when it crosses a line. You can feel it coming, which is the dread.

**5-minute: the sortie**
Fly the pod to a derelict → board → find one salvageable system (scrubber, reactor cell, hull plate, data core) → extract it under rising Attention → return → integrate it into the home-ship. Every derelict shows one visible unknown from outside, which is the "one more sortie" pull.

**Session (60–120 min)**
Pick a target on the web map, prep (O₂, tools, sanity suppressants), run 2–4 sorties, come home, integrate parts, re-stabilize the ship's loops, read the logs you pulled. Natural stop: the ship is stable again. The hook: the log you recovered names a deeper derelict.

**Progression (weeks)**
Home-ship capability (life-support margin, range, hull), **knowledge** (the web's rules, horror tells, decoded lore), **depth** (rings of the web), and crew **sanity scars** (permanent quirks a character carries). No win state. The center is a horizon, not a finish line.

**Motivation (SDT)**
- *Autonomy*: which derelict, which parts, how deep, and who boards vs. who keeps the ship alive.
- *Competence*: reading a failing system, surviving a breach, learning what each horror does before it does it.
- *Relatedness*: co-op roles, plus sanity is **per-player**, so you have to decide whether to trust a crewmate's readings. That's your Zomboid-base-with-friends moment, with teeth.

## Pillars (locked, autonomous)

1. **The Ship Is a Body** — every system is a visible loop you can watch failing; nothing fails silently.
   *Test*: hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe.
2. **Dread Before Chaos** — horror is earned through anticipation; chaos is the payoff, never the default.
   *Test*: jump-scare on boarding vs. a slow tell that escalates → the tell.
3. **The Web Watches** — your choices raise or lower its attention; restraint and stealth are real strategies.
   *Test*: flat spawn timer vs. attention-driven escalation → attention.
4. **Sanity Is Information** — low sanity changes what you *know*, not just your stats; gauges can lie.
   *Test*: −10% move speed vs. a gauge showing a false value → the false gauge.
5. **Deeper Is Richer** — risk and reward map to depth; there's no safe outer ring to farm forever.
   *Test*: safe farming vs. scarcity that pushes inward → scarcity.

Pillars 1 and 4 deliberately pull against each other (legible systems vs. lying readings). The resolution is itself a mechanic: the lie is visible *to a saner crewmate*.

**Anti-pillars**
- **NOT a freeform ship-building sandbox** — welding is functional, modules are pre-shaped; creative construction would dilute Dread and Depth.
- **NOT a combat game** — no weapon tree; horrors are avoided and survived, not farmed. Protects The Web Watches.
- **NOT an authored linear story** — no chapters or cutscenes; lore is found and assembled. Protects the long tail.
- **NOT PvP** — co-op only; sanity creates systemic distrust, not griefing. Protects Relatedness.
- **NOT a game you win** — no "escape the web" ending in v1.

Sending CD-PILLARS, AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL and TD-FEASIBILITY out together now (the feasibility gate's inputs are all known: PC, Godot 4.7.2 GDScript, solo first-timer).

- NOT a combat game (no weapon tree; horrors avoided/survived, not farmed) — protects The Web Watches.

input.prompt:
You are running gate TD-FEASIBILITY for /brainstorm. FIRST read `.claude/docs/director-gates/td-feasibility.md` (repo root: D:\the-synaptic-sea-2d) and follow its Prompt and Verdicts exactly. Also consult `docs/engine-reference/godot/VERSION.md` and `docs/engine-reference/godot/modules/networking.md` for the pinned engine before judging networking claims — do not rely on training-data knowledge of Godot 4.7. Return one verdict word from the gate file's Verdicts line (or NOT ASSESSED if an input is missing), with rationale and per-risk assessment.

Context to pass:

CORE LOOP: Co-op 2D offset-top-down survival sim. Players wake in a derelict ship's cryo bay, repair a podcraft, fly to procedurally generated derelicts trapped in a cosmic web, board them (slow, stealthy "boarding rhythm"), salvage functional modules (scrubbers, reactor cells, hull plates, data cores) and weld them onto a growing mobile home-ship whose life support (O2, heat, power) is a visible, continuously simulated system graph. The web accumulates "Attention" from player light/noise/power/depth; crossing thresholds flips play into a frantic "breach rhythm" (hull failure, power loss, horror awakening). Per-player sanity degrades with exposure; low sanity causes client-visible hallucinations INCLUDING false instrument readings that other (saner) players do not see. Progression: ship capability, knowledge, depth rings, permanent sanity scars. No win state; persistent long-tail play across many sessions.

PLATFORM TARGET: PC (Steam/Epic), Windows first.

ENGINE CHOICE: Godot 4.7.2 (stable), GDScript, Forward+ renderer, Godot Physics 2D. Pinned in project.yaml.

TEAM / TIMELINE: solo developer, first game, no prior engine experience, no fixed timeline (open-ended).

IDENTIFIED TECHNICAL RISKS:
1. Multiplayer netcode for a simulation-heavy game in Godot (high-level multiplayer API, authority model, who simulates the life-support graph, listen-server vs dedicated host, join-in-progress).
2. Modular ship as a composition of welded derelict sections — each section a scene with its own life-support nodes joined into one ship-wide graph; needs runtime attach/detach, hull integrity, and physics/collision of a composite body.
3. Procedural derelict generation that produces boardable, readable, salvage-bearing interiors (not noise) in 2D oblique perspective.
4. Per-player sanity-driven client-side misinformation: deliberately divergent rendering/UI between clients of the same authoritative state, while keeping the simulation itself in sync.
5. HD pixel-art pipeline: large detailed sprite sheets, 2D lighting/occlusion for dread (Forward+ 2D lights, shadows), performance with many lit sprites and particles.
6. Persistence of a mobile, player-composed base across sessions (save/load of a composite ship + world seed + web state), including when the host changes.
7. Solo first-time developer taking on all of the above.

Do not write any files. Return your verdict, rationale and per-risk notes as your final message.

content.text:
Decisions logged to `production/session-logs/decision-log.md`. The three directors are reviewing in the background. While they work, here's Phase 5:

## Who This Is For

**Primary: Explorers who like their systems to bite.** The Zomboid / Barotrauma / Oxygen Not Included crowd: players who read a failing machine as a puzzle and a dark corridor as a question. They want to *understand* the web more than beat it, and they'll tolerate slow pacing if the systems are honest and the dread pays off. Quantic Foundry would tag them high **Discovery + Strategy**, moderate **Excitement**, low **Competition**.

**Secondary: Socializers who want a crew.** Your own anchor moment. The per-player sanity design is really for them: a game that gives a group of friends a reason to talk ("is that reading real?") is a game they return to. Also **Achievers**, lightly: ship capability and depth rings give them a ladder, but there's no completion checklist to chase.

**Not for:**
- *Competitors / Killers* — no PvP, no leaderboards, horrors you avoid rather than farm.
- *Players who want authored narrative payoff* — lore is assembled from fragments; there's no ending.
- *Builders who want freeform creativity* — modules are pre-shaped; this isn't Space Engineers.
- *Anyone who needs fast onboarding* — the two-rhythm loop is slow by design.

**Market signal:** Project Zomboid (~200k concurrent peaks, a decade of EA), Barotrauma (co-op sub horror, >1M sold), Lethal Company (co-op dread, broke out from a solo dev), Oxygen Not Included (systems survival). Cosmic-horror survival has a hungry audience and almost no co-op systems-sim entries in it. That's the gap.

The scope question is the real one for a solo first-timer, and that's what the technical-director and producer gates are for. I'll report their verdicts when they land.

  **Summary.** These pillars hold up. All five can be tested and four can be failed by a real design choice. The 1-vs-4 tension is deliberate, which is the strongest thing in the set, and Pillars 3 and 4 set the game apart from Project Zomboid, Barotrauma and Dredge. I am not returning APPROVE for two reasons. First, the fix for the main tension depends on having a second player, and nothing has been decided for solo play or for two players who are both low on sanity. Second, two of the design tests set up an option nobody would argue for, so they won't settle a real disagreement. All of this can be fixed by sharpening the existing pillars. None of it needs a rethink.
  
  ---
  
  ### Per-pillar feedback
  
  **P1 — The Ship Is a Body.** Testable and useful. "Hidden stat vs leaking pipe" is a choice the team will actually face many times.
  - *Concern:* "Nothing fails silently" is absolute, and P4 breaks it on purpose. From the hallucinating player's point of view, a lying gauge is a silent failure. As written, P1 and P4 contradict each other, and a design review would have no way to decide between them.
  - *Sharpen:* Separate the physical world from instruments. Suggested rewording: "The physical world never lies. Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses. Only instruments and perception can be wrong." The leaking pipe becomes the ground truth and the gauge becomes the thing that can lie. This settles the 1-vs-4 tension inside the game world, even with no crewmate present.
  - *Differentiation:* On its own it is close to Barotrauma. It becomes distinctive when combined with the welded-from-dead-ships home-ship.
  
  **P2 — Dread Before Chaos.** The goal is right, but the design test is weak. Nobody on a team argues for jump-scares on boarding. The real arguments will be "how long can a breach build before it fires?" and "can a breach ever happen without warning?"
  - *Sharpen:* Turn it into a rule: "Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived (sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress)." A better test: "Breach triggers at a hidden threshold vs. breach preceded by a 10-30 second escalating tell → the tell."
  - *Overlap risk with P3:* Both are about escalation. Keep them apart. P2 covers tempo and presentation (how the escalation feels). P3 covers causality (what the player did to cause it). Write that split down, or reviewers will treat them as the same pillar.
  
  **P3 — The Web Watches.** This is the strongest pillar for the design itself. It is testable, it gives the player real choices (restraint as a strategy), and it constrains audio and lighting as much as game design.
  - *Concern:* Attention only works as strategy if players can read it, and that makes it a P1 obligation. The web's attention must show up in the world (creaking, light flicker, web movement) and must not be a hidden meter. Otherwise players will experience it as a flat spawn timer, which is the exact thing the pillar rejects.
  - *Tension to note:* Depth (P5) raises attention on its own, regardless of what the player does. Decide whether depth sets the *baseline* attention (my recommendation) or adds to it. If it adds, deep runs will feel like the player's choices don't matter.
  
  **P4 — Sanity Is Information.** This is the hook and the best differentiator in the set. Very few games make perception itself the resource you lose. It is testable, and the test is excellent.
  - *Concern 1 (critical):* Solo play and co-op where everyone is insane. The fix you've written ("visible to a saner crewmate") does nothing with one player, or once all players are low on sanity. You need a fallback that doesn't depend on another player: the physical ground truth from P1 (does the pipe actually leak?), cross-checking two instruments, or a manual check that takes time and risk. Decide now whether solo play is supported at all. If it isn't, say so in the pitch.
  - *Concern 2 (fairness):* If a false reading on a critical system leads to death with no way to detect the lie, players will call it cheap, and that hurts competence. Add a rule: "Every lie is detectable by someone or something. No hallucination is unfalsifiable."
  - *Note for the producer:* Co-op networking is a large scope item for a solo first-time developer. Showing different values to different players is the easy part. The co-op itself is the risk. That is not a pillar flaw, but it should be raised before prototyping.
  
  **P5 — Deeper Is Richer.** Testable ("no safe outer ring" is a real choice to enforce), and it supports the long tail. It sets the game apart least, since Subnautica, Dredge and Darkwood share this structure. That's acceptable, because this pillar holds up the game's structure more than its identity.
  - *Concern:* With no win state, permanent sanity scars and constant pressure inward, the long tail heads toward a death spiral. The pillar needs a stated failure contract. What happens when the home-ship dies or a crewmate's sanity collapses? Is it permadeath, a fallback to an earlier state, or carrying forward knowledge of the web's rules? "Deeper is richer" only motivates players if losing deep doesn't wipe out everything.
  - *Enforcement:* Say how outer-ring farming is prevented: depletion, rising attention, or scrubber parts that wear out. Without a stated mechanism, the pillar won't hold.
  
  ---
  
  ### Cross-cutting concerns
  
  1. **Co-op is load-bearing but has no pillar.** The core fantasy ("we're the only ones awake") and the P4 resolution both depend on crewmates. The only guarantee of co-op is the anti-pillar "NOT PvP". Either build relatedness into P4 explicitly ("...and crewmates are each other's instruments") or accept that co-op is a hook, not a pillar. My recommendation is to fold it into P4 and stay at five pillars.
  2. **"Starting to understand what that means".** The core fantasy promises gradual understanding through lore, but no pillar protects it. The "not authored linear story" anti-pillar covers it only partly. That's acceptable for v1, but make sure narrative work traces back to P4 (the shared question of what is real) and P5 (the deeper the players go, the truer the lore gets).
  3. **Anti-pillars are strong.** Each one names what it protects, which is good practice. One gap: "NOT a combat game" needs a line on whether there are non-weapon deterrents (flares, cutting torches, decoys). Otherwise designers will argue about where a tool ends and a weapon begins. A suggested rule: "Tools may repel or distract; nothing levels up from killing."
  
  ### Revisions needed for APPROVE
  1. Reword P1 so the physical world is ground truth and only instruments or perception can lie.
  2. Add a detection fallback to P4 that works solo and when all players are low on sanity, plus a "no unfalsifiable lies" rule.
  3. Replace P2's design test with one that settles a real disagreement (a hidden-threshold breach vs. a breach preceded by a tell).
  4. State how P2 and P3 divide the work, and how depth affects attention (baseline vs. adding on).
  5. Add a failure/continuity contract to P5.
  
  No files were written.
</agent-message>

The creative-director came back **CONCERNS** on the pillars, with specific, fixable notes rather than a rethink. In `autonomous` I'm taking the recommended path (revise the flagged items) and logging it. Here's what changed and why:

**Revised pillars**

1. **The World Never Lies** *(was "The Ship Is a Body")* — pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only instruments and perception can be wrong.
   *Test*: hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe. *This resolves the P1/P4 contradiction inside the game world, with or without a crewmate.*
2. **Dread Before Chaos** — every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived (sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress). P2 owns *tempo and presentation*; P3 owns *causality*.
   *Test*: breach fires at a hidden threshold vs. breach preceded by a 10–30 s escalating tell → the tell.
3. **The Web Watches** — the players' light, noise, power and restraint raise or lower its attention, and attention is **shown in the world** (creaking, flicker, web movement), never as a hidden meter. Depth sets the *baseline*; player action moves it from there.
   *Test*: flat spawn timer vs. attention-driven escalation → attention.
4. **Sanity Is Information, and Crewmates Are Instruments** — low sanity changes what you *know*; gauges can lie. **No lie is unfalsifiable**: every hallucination can be checked against the physical world, a second instrument, or a saner crewmate, and checking costs time or risk.
   *Test*: −10% speed vs. a false gauge → the false gauge. *Solo play is supported via the physical-world and second-instrument checks; co-op adds the human check.*
5. **Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total** — risk and reward map to depth, and the outer ring is kept unsafe by *depletion and wear* (scrubbers degrade, salvage runs out). **Failure contract**: losing the home-ship or a crewmate costs ship and body, never knowledge. Decoded web rules and lore persist; the next crew wakes knowing more.
   *Test*: safe farming vs. scarcity that pushes inward → scarcity.

**Anti-pillar addition**: *NOT a combat game* now reads: tools may repel or distract (flares, torches, decoys); **nothing levels up from killing.**

Sending the revision back to the creative-director for a re-check while the art and technical gates finish.

  TD-FEASIBILITY: HIGH RISK
  
  **Summary:** The concept is technically buildable in Godot 4.7.2. Nothing here argues for a different engine. Two parts of the concept as written need a scope change before this passes: (1) persistence "including when the host changes", and (2) building co-op, procgen, the composite ship and persistence all at once as a solo first-time developer. With the two changes below, the remaining risks are CONCERNS-grade, meaning they have standard engineering fixes that leave the concept text as it is. The core fantasy survives unchanged: derelict salvage, a welded mobile ship, a visible life-support graph, Attention and the two play rhythms, and sanity hallucinations.
  
  Sources checked: `.claude/docs/director-gates/td-feasibility.md`, `docs/engine-reference/godot/VERSION.md` (4.7.2 mono build installed, matches the pin), `modules/networking.md`, `modules/rendering.md`, `modules/physics.md`, `breaking-changes.md`, `project.yaml`.
  
  ---
  
  ## A. Blockers that need concept or scope changes
  
  **B1: Persistence across a change of host (Risk 6).** The pinned networking reference shows the high-level API as ENetMultiplayerPeer plus MultiplayerSpawner/MultiplayerSynchronizer plus SceneMultiplayer, with one server-authority peer. There are no documented networking changes from 4.5 through 4.7, and nothing for host migration. If the host leaves, the session ends. Supporting "the host changes" means one of:
  - building a custom migration layer: authority transfer, state handoff, re-spawning every replicated node. This is a large distributed-systems problem, unsuitable for a first game; or
  - **(recommended revision)** keeping the world in a single owner's save. Whoever owns the save hosts it, and co-op players are guests. A guest can later host the same world only by having the save file copied or exported to them. That is offline save portability, not live migration.
  
  This also raises a design question that is not mine to decide: **whose save owns the shared ship, and what do guests keep?** Examples: a personal copy of knowledge and sanity scars versus nothing. That goes to game-designer and creative-director.
  
  **B2: Order of building co-op versus everything else (Risk 7, linked to Risk 1).** Building co-op networking, a simulation graph, procedural generation, a composite physics body and persistence all at once is the classic way a solo first project stalls. Required revision, which is more than just reordering work:
  - From day one, design the game as server-authoritative with a single player. The local player is just "server plus one client" (Godot's listen-server pattern), so all simulation mutations go through authority-checked requests.
  - The first vertical slice is single-player only: one handmade derelict, a weld, the O2/heat/power graph, one Attention threshold.
  - **Online co-op is gated behind that slice**, and is not a launch requirement until the slice is fun. Co-op stays a feature, but it is no longer an up-front commitment.
  - Drop join-in-progress from the initial co-op scope. Lobby-start sessions first; joining mid-session later, built on the same save/snapshot code as B1.
  
  If you reject both changes, I would still score this HIGH RISK. If you accept them, I expect a re-run of this gate to return CONCERNS.
  
  ---
  
  ## B. Engine-specific risks (does any of this argue against Godot?)
  
  No. Godot 4.7 is a reasonable fit for a 2D co-op simulation, and its high-level multiplayer API fits a small-session listen-server game. Caveats to carry forward:
  - **D3D12 is the default rendering driver on Windows since 4.6** (it used to be Vulkan). You are Windows-first, so test 2D lighting and shaders on D3D12 early and know how to switch to Vulkan as a fallback if driver problems appear.
  - **Forward+ was chosen for a 2D game.** Fine, but 2D lighting goes through the canvas renderer, so Forward+ brings no special 2D benefit. Treat the renderer choice as reversible and measure before committing. Compatibility mode would widen low-end hardware support.
  - **In 4.7 the Asset Store replaces the Asset Library.** Any third-party netcode, lobby or Steam integration addon must be checked for 4.7 compatibility and availability through the new store. Steam lobbies and NAT traversal (e.g. a GodotSteam-style integration) need their own technology evaluation. ENet alone does not solve players connecting from behind home routers.
  - **The installed build is the mono (.NET) edition.** GDScript works fine in it. Note it for the export setup only.
  - **2D physics is still Godot Physics 2D.** The 4.6/4.7 Jolt changes are 3D-only and don't affect you.
  - 4.5–4.7 are past the model's training cutoff. Every API claim must be checked against `docs/engine-reference/godot/`, as this assessment did.
  
  ---
  
  ## C. Risks solo developers commonly underestimate
  
  1. **NAT traversal and lobbies.** "Co-op works on LAN" and "co-op works for Steam friends" are separate milestones.
  2. **Save-format versioning.** A game with no win state and many sessions will break saves every time a module's data changes. Version saves and write migrations from the first save file.
  3. **Debugging desync.** Divergent hallucinations (Risk 4) and authoritative state that has actually drifted out of sync look the same to a tester. You need a debug overlay that shows the true values, from the start.
  4. **Readable procedural content.** Making generated content readable takes far longer than the generator itself.
  5. **Art throughput.** Detailed HD pixel art for modular derelict sections is probably the largest time sink of the project, larger than the code.
  6. **Testing a multiplayer game alone.** Plan for running several local instances (Godot's debug run supports several instances) and scripted bot clients.
  
  ---
  
  ## Per-risk assessment
  
  **1. Multiplayer netcode / authority: MEDIUM-HIGH, manageable with B2.** The host simulates the whole life-support graph at a fixed tick. Clients send requests through any_peer RPCs, the server validates them and broadcasts the result. This matches the server-authoritative pattern in networking.md. Replicate the graph's summary state (per-compartment O2/heat/power plus edge states) at low frequency, not every node every frame. Use reliable RPCs for structural events (weld, breach, module destroyed) and unreliable sync for positions. Host plus a few peers on ENet is well within the API's design envelope. Main open items: NAT traversal and lobbies, plus join-in-progress (deferred).
  
  **2. Modular welded ship / composite body: MEDIUM.** Known pattern: one physics root body for the ship, with each section's collision shapes and life-support nodes reparented under it when welded and split off into a new body when detached. Keep the life-support graph as a pure data model (resources or plain objects) that the scene nodes register with, not something you get by walking the scene tree. That lets you test it headlessly and serialize it, and it turns hull integrity into graph properties. Spike first: weld and detach two sections, mid-flight, with the graph recomputing.
  
  **3. Procedural derelicts: MEDIUM.** Avoid pure noise. Hallucination state is never sent as game state and never feeds back into requests the server accepts as fact.   AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL: CONCEPTS
  
  **Rationale for verdict.** The five pillars are rich enough to drive three genuinely distinct directions inside the user's fixed medium (high-definition pixel art, 3/4 oblique top-down). None collapses into another: they resolve the Pillar 1 vs Pillar 3 tension (legibility wants light; attention punishes light) three different ways. Each is viable against the cross-cutting Pillar 4 constraint, which is the real filter: "gauges can lie" only works if the baseline visual language is trustworthy enough for a lie to be noticed. Every direction names what drifts under low sanity and what stays fixed as the player's calibration anchor. I recommend Direction A; the choice is the user's.
  
  Primary pillar treated as Pillar 1 (The Ship Is a Body, listed first). Direction A serves it directly.
  
  ---
  
  ### Direction A — "Every Pipe Is a Sentence" (serves Pillar 1 directly)
  
  **Visual rule:** If it works, you can see it working; if it fails, you can see exactly where.
  
  **Mood / atmosphere:** A warm, hand-maintained workshop floating in a cold indifferent void. Project Zomboid's lived-in clutter meets Satisfactory's legible flows. The ship is the only honest thing in the universe; the horror is that the honesty erodes (Pillar 4). Interior reads as "ours" the moment power is on.
  
  **Shape language:** Hard separation of two vocabularies. Human/mechanical = rectilinear hull plates, cylindrical pipes, round valves and gauges, rounded fittings, 90- and 45-degree runs that respect the 3/4 grid (vertical runs on walls, horizontal on floor). Web = filamentous, branching, never a straight line, never a right angle. The player's rule: anything organic is not yours. Salvaged modules from other ships keep the mechanical vocabulary but carry a different manufacturer "dialect" (plate rhythm, bolt spacing) so welded additions visibly read as grafts.
  
  **Supporting principles with design tests:**
  1. *State lives in the sprite, not the icon.* Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (fluid, spark, airflow). Test: a pump with a green/red status LED vs a pump with a turning rotor and visible fluid in its pipe → rotor and fluid. The LED may exist, but it is never the only tell.
  2. *Failure is a trail, not a flag.* Damage renders as a path the eye can follow back to source: leak puddles, scorch, frost, pressure mist, in the loop's hue. Test: a flashing "COOLANT LOW" warning vs a frosted pipe elbow with a slow drip → the frosted elbow (the warning is the gauge that can lie; the frost is the body that cannot, at least at high sanity).
  3. *Light is emission, and emission is exposure.* With power off, the ship is lit only by the glow of its own loops, so the player reads their ship in the dark by what is running. Test: a flat dark "unpowered" ambient vs loops glowing in their own hue while the hull goes cold blue → the glowing loops. This resolves Pillar 1 vs 3: you can always read the loops, and every loop you run is a lantern the web can see.
  
  **Color philosophy:** Flow-coded. Each resource loop owns a hue and keeps it everywhere it appears: pipe medium, gauge, HUD readout, leak. Working proposal: oxygen cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, structure/integrity neutral grey, web attention violet-magenta (the one hue no human system uses). Interior under power: warm tungsten pools with soft falloff. Interior unpowered: cold blue-black steel, loops self-lit. Exterior/void: near-black with the web's violet filaments as the only chroma, brightening and reaching toward the player's light sources as attention rises (Pillar 3 made visible). Deeper rings darken and desaturate the ambient toward graphite rather than tinting it; saturated violet-magenta is reserved for filaments and for the sanity bleed below, so saturated violet on a pipe always means sanity, never location (Pillar 5 reads as denser filaments, not a purple room).
  *Sanity shift:* instruments drift first. Gauge needles and HUD readouts show readings that disagree with the body of the ship; at lower sanity the loop hues themselves begin to bleed toward violet at the edges of the pipe medium (independent of ambient), and flow animation stutters on pipes that are actually fine. *Anchor that never shifts:* hull geometry, character sprites, and the HUD frame itself. The player learns to trust their eyes over their instruments, then learns that even that trust has a floor. Accessibility coordination point for ux-designer (not decided here): hue coding must be redundant with shape/pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) for colorblind players.
  
  **Pipeline cost:** Highest tile/prop state count (each system needs idle, running, failing, leaking, dead), lowest lighting complexity. Flow animation can be shader-driven rather than hand-framed (technical-artist call), which recovers most of the frame cost.
  
  ---
  
  ### Direction B — "The Dark Is the Default"
  
  **Visual rule:** Light is a resource you spend; everything you can see, you paid for.
  
  **Mood / atmosphere:** Barotrauma and Pandorum. Claustrophobic, flashlight-cone, oppressive black broken by hard pools of detail. The ship is a cave you keep partially lit. Dread comes from what the light does not reach and from the moment you must choose to turn it on (Pillars 2 and 3).
  
  **Shape language:** Heavy, angular industrial brutalism. Thick bulkheads, hard shadows, deep recesses that hide things. The web is not rendered as a shape at distance: it is hairline filaments that read as cracks in the black, only resolving into form when caught in the player's light, where it shows a faint oily iridescence. Horror by negative space.
  
  **Supporting principles with design tests:**
  1. *Darkness is honest; light is a decision.* Rooms are not fogged, they are unlit; the geometry is there and will be revealed by any source. Test: a vignette/fog-of-war mask vs true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff → true occlusion.
  2. *Failing systems announce themselves by emitting.* Because the default is dark, any system in trouble must become a light source (sparks, heat glow, warning strobe). Test: a silent dark broken pump vs a dark pump throwing intermittent blue sparks that light the surrounding hull → the sparks. This is B's only route to Pillar 1 and is its structural risk: healthy systems are hard to read in the dark.
  3. *Attention is a reflection.* The web is seen only in the player's own light: the brighter you run, the more filaments resolve, the closer they appear. Test: an attention meter vs more filaments becoming visible in your light cone as attention rises → the filaments.
  
  **Color philosophy:** Near-monochrome cold base (blue-black steel, graphite) with exactly two warm accents: human light (tungsten amber) and alarm (red). The web has no hue of its own; it is absence, with an oily iridescence under direct light. Deeper rings do not change hue; they reduce ambient further and raise the iridescence (Pillar 5 as a darker, glossier dark).
  *Sanity shift:* the light lies. Your cone appears to reach further than it does, shadows render where no occluder exists, light temperature cools or warms without cause. Readouts flicker between two values. *Anchor that never shifts:* character sprites, hand tools, and the physical radius of what your light actually reveals when you walk into it.
  
  **Pipeline cost:** Lowest tile/prop variant count (dark hides repetition), highest lighting and normal-map load for high-res pixel art; feasible in Godot 4 2D lighting but it becomes the technical-artist's main workload, and co-op readability of a partner's dark ship section is a known cost.
  
  ---
  
  ### Direction C — "The Ship Grows a Nervous System"
  
  **Visual rule:** The deeper you go, the less your ship looks like a machine.
  
  **Mood / atmosphere:** Beyond the Aquila Rift and Stellaris's slow-reveal horror. Bodily uncanny, horror by accretion. The game begins clean-industrial and ends with a ship that has veins. Salvage from the inner web is better and wronger, so the player's own home becomes the escalating tell (Pillars 2 and 5).
  
  **Shape language:** A gradient indexed to depth. Outer-ring salvage is rectilinear, symmetrical, clean. Inner-ring salvage carries sinew-like cabling, bulbous asymmetric fittings, housings that look grown around their mechanism. Web filaments are drawn as neurons: nodes, dendritic branching, synaptic gaps that flash when attention fires, making the title literal. Pipes already read as veins, so Pillar 1's "body" metaphor is drawn, not implied.
  
  **Supporting principles with design tests:**
  1. *Salvage carries its depth with it.* Any module can be read at a glance for where in the web it came from by how organic its silhouette is. Test: a depth-tier number on the module tooltip vs the module visibly more organic → the shape.
  2. *Two axes, never one.* Depth drifts shape; sanity drifts color and motion. Kept on separate axes so the player can disentangle "this module is from deep" from "I am seeing things." Test: deep salvage that also pulses and hue-shifts at full sanity vs deep salvage that is organic in silhouette but painted in the same stable steel/loop palette until sanity drops → color-stable. This principle is what keeps C viable against Pillar 4.
  3. *The web fires, it does not swarm.* Attention is shown as synaptic pulses travelling along filaments toward the player, brightening at the nodes. Test: more enemies spawning vs the filament pulse frequency rising → the pulse.
  
  **Color philosophy:** Depth is carried by the web and the void, never by the ship. Outer ring: near-black void, sparse filaments. Inner rings: the void saturates with the web's own bioluminescence until the ambient chroma belongs to the web rather than to humans. Salvage modules and loop hues stay color-stable at every depth; only silhouette carries depth. content.text:
Got it: **B-dominant, with A's legibility inside the light.** And the hallucination intensity you describe changes the design more than the art, so I'm folding it in properly rather than just noting it.

**Visual Identity Anchor — "What You Light, You Can Read"**
*Rule*: Light is a resource you spend. Inside your light, every pipe is a sentence (A's flow-coded legibility, failure as a visible trail). Outside it, the dark is honest and the web is only ever seen in your own glow. Loops self-illuminate when running, so a working system is both readable and exposed. Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world, so when they appear, it's you.

**Pillar 4 upgraded** — "Sanity Is Information" becomes **"Sanity Rewrites Reality"**. Hallucination classes, from the top of the list:
- *Phantom entities*: monsters that aren't there (and, at depth, real ones that get hidden).
- *False system states*: broken things read as fixed, fixed as broken — the gauge lie, now extended to the sprite itself.
- *Crewmates as monsters*: a teammate renders as a horror. Friendly harm is possible, so the stakes are real.
- *Phantom salvage*: a crate of treasure that's garbage when you get it home.

The falsifiability rule stays, but it becomes **costly** rather than easy: the truth is always available through the physical world, a second instrument, a saner crewmate, or *time* (the crate reveals itself at home). Design test: *hallucination that can never be disproved vs. one that costs time, risk or trust to disprove → the costly one.* The TD's "one channel at a time" rule becomes "at least one channel of truth remains," and the anti-pillars adjust: **NOT PvP** now reads "no *intentional* PvP; harm to crewmates is only ever a sanity failure," and **nothing levels up from killing** still holds. I'll re-run CD-PILLARS on these at the end, since it's a real change to the approved set.

**Cost honesty**: a B-dominant look means the lighting pipeline is the main art workload, exactly what the TD and the producer flagged. Shadow-casting 2D lights need to be few, and the lighting-budget spike moves from "important" to "first."

---

**PR-SCOPE: OPTIMISTIC.** The producer's read: the MVP feature list is well-disciplined (that's what kept it from UNREALISTIC), but 4–6 months ignores the Godot learning curve (~1–3 months) and the authority-layer tax. Honest MVP range: **6–9 months full-time, 10–16 part-time**. The bigger problem is the Vertical Slice tier: it bundles procgen, co-op *and* target art, so if co-op eats the months, the fallback is a broken product rather than a small solo game. And the tier arithmetic leaves 0–24 months for the whole Full Vision tier, which can't be right. These are scope changes, so they're yours:

# Game Concept: The Synaptic Sea

*Created: 2026-10-25*
*Status: Draft*

> **Creative Director Review (CD-PILLARS)**: APPROVED 2026-10-25 (five-pillar revision) — re-check pending on the Pillar 4 intensity upgrade
> **Art Director Review (AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL)**: DIRECTIONS DELIVERED 2026-10-25 — user selected a B-dominant hybrid (see Visual Identity Anchor)
> **Technical Director Review (TD-FEASIBILITY)**: CONCERNS (accepted) 2026-10-25 — HIGH RISK as first written; two scope changes accepted (host-owned save, single-player slice first)
> **Producer Review (PR-SCOPE)**: OPTIMISTIC → adjustments applied 2026-10-25 (VS split, spike phase, widened MVP estimate, 4–6 year horizon)

---

## Elevator Pitch

> It's a co-op survival sim where you keep a ship welded together from dead ships
> alive inside a vast cosmic web, and the deeper you salvage, the less you can
> trust what you see.

Wake in the cryo bay of a derelict. Repair a podcraft. Board the other wrecks
caught in the web, strip their working systems, weld them onto your own hull.
The web notices light and noise. Exposure erodes sanity, and sanity rewrites
what your eyes and instruments tell you.

---

## Core Identity

| Aspect | Detail |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Genre** | Survival sim / cosmic horror, with functional (not freeform) base-building |
| **Platform** | PC (Steam / Epic), Windows first |
| **Target Audience** | Systems-literate explorers who want co-op dread (see Player Profile) |
| **Player Count** | 1–4. Single-player first; online co-op gated behind the proven slice |
| **Session Length** | 60–120 minutes |
| **Monetization** | Premium, Early Access (provisional — not yet decided) |
| **Estimated Scope** | Large (48–72 months, solo) |
| **Comparable Titles** | Project Zomboid, Barotrauma, Oxygen Not Included |

---

## Core Fantasy

"The ship is alive because we keep it alive, minute by minute — and we're the
only ones awake, and we're starting to understand what that means."

Cooperative self-sufficiency under cosmic dread. The player's base is not a
house they found; it is a body they assembled from the corpses of other ships,
and every loop in it is something they personally keep breathing. The horror
is not that the web attacks the ship. It is that the web attacks the crew's
ability to know whether the ship is fine.

The emotional anchor comes directly from the designer's own touchstone: a
Project Zomboid base, built with friends, that becomes self-sufficient and
survivable. This game puts that feeling in a place where "survivable" is never
quite certain and the friends might be hallucinating.

---

## Unique Hook

Like Project Zomboid's long-tail survival loop, **AND ALSO** your base is a
life-support machine welded from other dead ships, and the sanity system is a
perception system: gauges, sprites, salvage and even your crewmates can lie to
you, and the only cure is to check — which costs time, risk or trust.

Why it is not a gimmick:
- It affects gameplay, not aesthetics. A false "fixed" state on a scrubber is
  a death you walked into.
- It is connected to the core fantasy. Co-op matters because crewmates are each
  other's instruments.
- It is novel. Sanity in survival games is usually a stat debuff. Here it is
  misinformation with a verification economy around it.

---

## Player Experience Analysis (MDA Framework)

### Target Aesthetics (What the player FEELS)

| Aesthetic | Priority | How We Deliver It |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Discovery** (exploration, secrets) | 1 | Procedural derelicts with one visible unknown each; web rules learned by observation; lore assembled from fragments; the center as a horizon |
| **Challenge** (obstacle course, mastery) | 2 | Visible life-support graph that fails in traceable ways; Attention management; breach recovery; learning horror tells |
| **Fellowship** (social connection) | 3 | Crew roles (boarder vs. ship-keeper); per-player sanity makes trust a mechanic; a shared home-ship |
| **Fantasy** (make-believe) | 4 | "We are the only ones awake"; a ship that is ours because we welded it |
| **Narrative** (drama, story arc) | 5 | Non-linear lore; the cryo-bay question (who else is in the pods, and why do they keep waking?) |
| **Sensation** (sensory pleasure) | 6 | HD pixel art under a light-as-resource rendering model; flow-coded loops glowing in the dark; adaptive audio (later tier) |
| **Expression** (self-expression) | 7 | Which modules to graft and where — functional, not cosmetic |
| **Submission** (relaxation) | N/A | Deliberately absent |

### Key Dynamics (Emergent player behaviors)

- Players will **go dark** deliberately — running fewer loops, cutting lights —
  to lower the web's attention before a deep sortie.
- Players will **cross-check each other**: "Is that scrubber really green on
  your screen?" becomes normal crew chatter.
- Players will **specialize**: one keeps the ship alive, one boards.
- Players will **weigh a module's value against the noise of taking it**.
- Players will **develop house rules for low-sanity crewmates** (disarm them,
  keep them away from the reactor) without the game prescribing it.
- Players will **tell stories about the time the loot was garbage**.

### Core Mechanics (Systems we build)

1. **Life-support graph** — O₂, heat and power as a continuously simulated,
   visible graph across welded sections; failures propagate along edges and
   render as physical trails (frost, mist, scorch, drip).
2. **Modular welding** — derelict sections are grafted onto the home-ship,
   joining their nodes to the graph and their collision to one composite body;
   sections can be cut away.
3. **Attention** — the web accumulates attention from light, noise, power use
   and depth (depth sets the baseline); shown in the world, never as a hidden
   meter; crossing thresholds flips boarding into breach.
4. **Sanity and hallucination** — per-player sanity degrades with exposure;
   low sanity drives a client-side presentation filter that corrupts perception
   (entities, system states, crewmates, salvage) while the simulation stays
   authoritative and at least one channel of truth remains.
5. **Procedural derelicts** — hand-authored room kits assembled by a generator
   from a seed, with salvage placed by rules and one externally visible
   unknown per wreck.
6. **Persistence and the failure contract** — host-owned, versioned saves of
   the composite ship, world seed plus deltas, and per-player progression;
   losing the ship or a body never loses knowledge.

---

## Player Motivation Profile

### Primary Psychological Needs Served

| Need | How This Game Satisfies It | Strength |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Autonomy** | Which derelict, which module, how deep, how loud, who boards and who stays | Core |
| **Competence** | Reading a failing loop, surviving a breach, learning what each horror does before it does it, learning when to doubt your eyes | Core |
| **Relatedness** | Crew roles; crewmates as each other's instruments; a shared ship; the cryo-bay mystery | Core (co-op), Supporting (solo via the ship-as-body) |

### Player Type Appeal (Bartle Taxonomy)

- [x] **Explorers** — Primary. Understanding the web's rules, the derelicts' stories, and their own perception.
- [x] **Socializers** — Secondary. Crew trust, verification chatter, shared stories of disaster.
- [x] **Achievers** — Light. Ship capability and depth rings as a ladder; no completion checklist.
- [ ] **Killers/Competitors** — Not served. No PvP, no leaderboards; horrors are avoided, not farmed.

### Flow State Design

- **Onboarding curve**: The cryo bay is a single sealed section with one
  failing loop. The first ten minutes teach "see the leak, follow it to the
  source, fix it, watch the gauge agree with the pipe." The first pod hop
  teaches the boarding rhythm; the first Attention threshold teaches breach.
- **Difficulty scaling**: Depth rings raise the Attention baseline, horror
  variety and salvage value together. Outer-ring depletion pushes inward.
- **Feedback clarity**: Every system has a visible moving part and medium.
  Failure is a trail the eye can follow. Attention is heard and seen before it
  acts. Sanity drift starts with instruments disagreeing with the world.
- **Recovery from failure**: Breach is survivable by retreat to the pod. Losing
  the ship or a crewmate loses ship and body, never knowledge: the next crew
  wakes in the cryo bay knowing more. Failure is educational by contract.

---

## Core Loop

### Moment-to-Moment (30 seconds) — two rhythms

- **Boarding rhythm** (deliberate, Zomboid-paced): cut a hatch, listen, sweep a
  light, read a dead ship's gauges, decide whether a module is worth the noise
  of taking it. Every door is a decision.
- **Breach rhythm** (frantic, Barotrauma-paced): the web has noticed. A hull
  section fails, power drops, something wakes. Patch, re-route, retreat.
- **The hinge** is Attention. Light, noise, power spikes and depth raise it; it
  is shown in the world; crossing a line flips the rhythm. Dread is feeling it
  come.

### Short-Term (5–15 minutes) — the sortie

Fly the pod to a derelict → board → find one salvageable system (scrubber,
reactor cell, hull plate, data core) → extract it under rising Attention →
return → weld it in. Every wreck shows one visible unknown from outside; that
is the "one more sortie" pull.

### Session-Level (60–120 minutes)

Pick a target on the web map. Prep (O₂, tools, suppressants). Run 2–4 sorties.
Come home, integrate modules, re-stabilize the graph, read recovered logs.
Natural stop: the ship is stable again. The hook: the log names a deeper wreck.

### Long-Term Progression (days/weeks)

- **Ship capability** — life-support margin, range, hull.
- **Knowledge** — the web's rules, horror tells, decoded lore. Persists across
  crew loss. Some rules shift with depth so the web never becomes solvable.
- **Depth** — rings of the web, each with a higher Attention baseline.
- **Sanity scars** — permanent quirks a character carries.
- There is no win state. The center is a horizon.

### Retention Hooks

- **Curiosity**: the unknown on every wreck; the log that names a deeper one;
  who else is in the cryo pods.
- **Investment**: a ship that is literally assembled from your history.
- **Social**: a crew that needs you to be the sane one tonight.
- **Mastery**: reading the graph faster; knowing a tell; knowing when to doubt.

---

## Game Pillars

### Pillar 1: The World Never Lies
Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only
instruments and perception can be wrong.

*Design test*: a hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe.

### Pillar 2: Dread Before Chaos
Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived
(sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress). This pillar owns tempo and
presentation; Pillar 3 owns causality.

*Design test*: breach fires at a hidden threshold vs. breach preceded by a
10–30 second escalating tell → the tell.

### Pillar 3: The Web Watches
The players' light, noise, power use and restraint raise or lower its
attention. Attention is shown in the world (creaking, flicker, filament
movement), never as a hidden meter. Depth sets the baseline; player action
moves it from there. Restraint and stealth are real strategies.

*Design test*: a flat spawn timer vs. attention-driven escalation → attention.

### Pillar 4: Sanity Rewrites Reality (and Crewmates Are Instruments)
Low sanity changes what the player perceives, not just their stats. Phantom
entities appear (and at depth, real ones hide). Broken things read as fixed and
fixed as broken. Crewmates render as horrors, and friendly harm is possible. A
crate of treasure is garbage once it is home. **No lie is unfalsifiable**: the
truth is always available through the physical world, a second instrument, a
saner crewmate, or time — and checking costs time, risk or trust. At least one
channel of truth always remains. Solo play is supported through the first two
checks; co-op adds the human one.

*Design test*: a hallucination that can never be disproved vs. one that costs
time, risk or trust to disprove → the costly one.
*Secondary test*: −10% move speed vs. a gauge showing a false value → the
false gauge.

### Pillar 5: Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total
Risk and reward map to depth in the web. The outer ring is kept unsafe by
depletion and wear (scrubbers degrade, salvage runs out), so there is no safe
place to farm forever. **Failure contract**: losing the home-ship or a crewmate
costs ship and body, never knowledge — decoded rules and lore persist, and the
next crew wakes knowing more.

*Design test*: safe farming vs. scarcity that pushes inward → scarcity.

**Intended tension**: Pillar 1 (legible) vs. Pillar 4 (lying). Resolved inside
the game world: the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception
are what can be wrong. The tension is the game.

### Anti-Pillars (What This Game Is NOT)

- **NOT a freeform ship-building sandbox**: welding is functional and modules
  are pre-shaped. Creative construction would dilute Dread Before Chaos and
  Deeper Is Richer.
- **NOT a combat game**: no weapon tree. Tools may repel or distract (flares,
  torches, decoys); nothing levels up from killing — including crewmates.
  Horrors are avoided and survived, not farmed. Protects The Web Watches.
- **NOT intentional PvP**: harm to a crewmate is only ever a sanity failure,
  never a system the game rewards. Protects relatedness.
- **NOT an authored linear story**: no chapters or cutscenes; lore is found and
  assembled. Protects the long tail.
- **NOT a game you win**: no "escape the web" ending in v1.

---

## Visual Identity Anchor

**Direction name**: *What You Light, You Can Read* — a B-dominant hybrid of the
art-director's "The Dark Is the Default" and "Every Pipe Is a Sentence".

**One-line visual rule**: Light is a resource you spend; inside your light,
every pipe is a sentence; outside it, the dark is honest.

**Supporting visual principles**

1. *Darkness is honest; light is a decision.* Rooms are not fogged, they are
   unlit; geometry is there and any source reveals it.
   *Test*: a vignette / fog-of-war mask vs. true 2D occlusion from light
   sources with hard falloff → true occlusion.
2. *Inside the light, state lives in the sprite, not the icon.* Every system
   has a visible moving part and medium; failure renders as a trail (puddle,
   frost, scorch, mist) in the loop's hue.
   *Test*: a status LED vs. a turning rotor with visible fluid → rotor and
   fluid; a "COOLANT LOW" banner vs. a frosted elbow with a drip → the elbow.
3. *Emission is exposure.* Running loops glow in their own hue; with power off
   the ship is lit only by what is running. Every loop you run is a lantern the
   web can see; the web itself is seen only in your own light.
   *Test*: an attention meter vs. more filaments resolving in your light cone
   as attention rises → the filaments.

**Color philosophy**: Near-monochrome cold base (blue-black steel, graphite).
Human light is tungsten amber; alarm is red. Resource loops are flow-coded and
keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O₂ cyan, power amber,
coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey). The web has an oily
iridescence under direct light and otherwise no hue of its own. Deeper rings
do not change hue; they lower ambient and raise the iridescence. **Flesh tones
and violet appear nowhere in the sane world**, so when they appear, it is the
player's sanity, never the location.

**Sanity drift**: instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the
ship), then the light lies (cone reaches further than it does, shadows with no
occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at the pipe edges
and flesh tones enter. **Anchors that never shift**: character sprites, hand
tools, the HUD frame, and the physical radius your light actually reveals when
you walk into it.

**Accessibility coordination** (for `/ux-design`): hue coding must be
redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) for colorblind
players.

**Pipeline note**: this direction puts the main art workload into the 2D
lighting pipeline rather than sprite-state count. The lighting-budget spike is
therefore the first spike, not the last.

## Inspiration and References

| Reference | What We Take From It | What We Do Differently | Why It Matters |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| Project Zomboid | Long-tail survival, lived-in detail, "one more day", base-with-friends | The base is mobile, modular, and made of other ships; no neighbourhoods | Validates patience for slow systemic survival and a decade-long EA model |
| Satisfactory | Legible machinery; flows you can read at a glance | The "factory" is a life-support system under eldritch pressure; no scale-up | Validates that watching a machine work is its own reward |
| Stellaris | Slow-reveal galactic horror; a universe that gets worse the more you know | Scale is one ship, not an empire; horror is personal and perceptual | Validates appetite for cosmic dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes |
| Barotrauma | Co-op crew under pressure in a hostile medium; breach rhythm | Boarding rhythm is slow and quiet; sanity is misinformation, not a stat | Validates co-op dread in a 2D vessel |
| Oxygen Not Included | Visible gas/heat/power simulation as the core puzzle | Far smaller graph, in service of dread rather than optimization | Validates a visible life-support graph as a core mechanic |

**Non-game inspirations**: *Beyond the Aquila Rift* (Love, Death & Robots) —
a ship trapped in a web, reality decaying, the kindness of the lie. *Pandorum*
— waking into wrongness aboard a derelict, not knowing how long you slept.

## Target Player Profile

| Attribute | Detail |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Age range** | 20–40 |
| **Gaming experience** | Mid-core to hardcore; comfortable with systems and slow pacing |
| **Time availability** | 1–2 hour evening sessions, often scheduled with friends; longer on weekends |
| **Platform preference** | PC, Steam |
| **Current games they play** | Project Zomboid, Barotrauma, Oxygen Not Included, Lethal Company |
| **What they're looking for** | Co-op dread with honest systems; a base that is theirs; a mystery that systems reveal, not cutscenes |
| **What would turn them away** | Jump-scare horror; fast onboarding expectations; freeform creative building; authored endings; PvP |

**Who this is NOT for**: competitors (no PvP or leaderboards), players who
want authored narrative payoff, freeform builders, anyone who needs a fast
start.
