## Technical Considerations

| Consideration | Assessment |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Recommended Engine** | Godot 4.7.2, GDScript (pinned by `/setup-engine`). TD-FEASIBILITY: nothing argues for another engine; high-level multiplayer fits a small listen-server co-op |
| **Key Technical Challenges** | Composite welded ship (one physics body, sections reparented on weld); life-support graph as pure data separate from the scene tree; server-authoritative design from day one even in single-player; per-client hallucination presentation filter that never touches the simulation; readable procgen from room kits; 2D lighting budget on D3D12 (Windows default since 4.6); versioned saves from v1 |
| **Art Style** | HD pixel art (high-resolution, detailed pixels), 3/4 oblique top-down, light-as-resource rendering |
| **Art Pipeline Complexity** | High — lighting pipeline is the main workload; modular derelict sections are the largest asset sink |
| **Audio Needs** | Adaptive (later tier). Attention and breach tells are audio-first; the ship must breathe |
| **Networking** | Listen-server (host-authoritative) via Godot high-level multiplayer. Host-owned saves, no live host migration. Steam lobby / NAT solution requires a technology evaluation before co-op work. Co-op gated behind the single-player slice |
| **Content Volume** | Full vision: 3 depth rings; several hand-authored room kits; dozens of module types; 4+ horror types; 4 hallucination classes; lore fragment set. Open-ended play; no fixed hours |
| **Procedural Systems** | Derelict interiors from kits + grammar, seeded; salvage placement by rules; host sends seed + deltas |

---

## Risks and Open Questions

### Design Risks
- The two-rhythm loop may not be tense and absorbing for 30+ minutes solo
  (the MVP's single question).
- Intense hallucinations may read as cheap deaths if the cost-to-verify is
  tuned wrong. "No lie is unfalsifiable" must hold in practice, not just on
  paper.
- Crewmates-as-monsters could become griefing-by-proxy without a guard rail
  (pending CD re-check).
- Persistent knowledge could make the web solvable; some rules must shift
  with depth.
- Deep resource simulation could swallow the dread (the Hull Pressure risk).

### Technical Risks (from TD-FEASIBILITY, CONCERNS)
- Authority discipline lapsing during the single-player phase → co-op becomes
  a rewrite. Enforce via ADR and control manifest; periodically run two local
  instances.
- Life-support graph entangled with the scene tree → untestable, unserializable.
- Save format not versioned from v1 → breaks every time a module changes.
- 2D lighting cost unmeasured for 4.7 on D3D12; Forward+ vs. Compatibility
  renderer is reversible and should be decided from spike data.
- Hallucination filter touching simulation state → endless desync bugs. Rule:
  every client receives the true value; corruption is presentation-only, with
  at least one channel of truth remaining, and a true-value debug overlay.
- Steam lobby / NAT traversal is a separate milestone from LAN co-op.
- 4.5–4.7 APIs are past the model's training cutoff; verify against
  `docs/engine-reference/godot/`.

### Market Risks
- Cosmic-horror survival is a niche within a niche; premium EA depends on a
  strong demo and word of mouth.
- Co-op arriving late may disappoint the audience most drawn to the pitch.

### Scope Risks (from PR-SCOPE, OPTIMISTIC → adjusted)
- First game, first engine: 1–3 months of learning folded into the MVP clock.
- HD pixel art throughput likely exceeds code time.
- No velocity data exists; every estimate is low-confidence until the spike
  phase produces some.
- Motivation over a 4–6 year solo horizon, not a deadline, is the real risk.

### Open Questions
- **What do guests keep** from a host-owned world (knowledge? sanity scars?
  nothing?) — for game-designer and creative-director; the save schema waits on
  it.
- **Who is in the other cryo pods, and why do they keep waking?** — for
  narrative-director; it is the failure contract's fiction.
- **Guard rail for crewmates-as-monsters** — pending CD-PILLARS re-check.
- **Renderer choice** (Forward+ vs. Compatibility) — answered by the lighting
  spike.
- **Steam lobby / NAT solution** — technology evaluation before VS-B.

---

## MVP Definition

**Core hypothesis**: The boarding→breach two-rhythm loop, over a visible
life-support graph, is tense and absorbing for a 30+ minute solo session.

**Required for MVP** (single-player):
1. One handmade spawn derelict and one handmade target derelict, with an
   abstracted pod hop between them.
2. Visible O₂ / heat / power graph with propagating, physically rendered
   failures.
3. One weld: attach one section and join its nodes to the graph.
4. Attention with one threshold and one horror behaviour.
5. Sanity as a single hallucination class (false system state), falsifiable by
   the physical world.
6. Save/load v1 with a format version.
7. All state changes through a single command/simulation layer (no networking
   code, no replication).

**Explicitly NOT in MVP**: procedural generation, co-op, multiple horrors,
other hallucination classes, lore, Steam, art at final fidelity, adaptive
audio.

**Kill/continue gate at the end of MVP**: playtest with at least three people
outside the project. If a 30+ minute solo session is not tense and absorbing,
iterate on the loop before any VS-A work. No procgen on an unproven loop.

### Scope Tiers (if budget/time shrinks)

| Tier | Content | Features | Timeline (solo; low confidence until spikes produce velocity) |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Spike phase** | Throwaway prototypes | Weld on a moving ship (tilemap + collision + graph merge); graph with spreading failures; save round-trip with version; 2D lighting budget on D3D12 | 4–8 weeks |
| **MVP** | 2 handmade derelicts | Core loop only (list above) + playtest gate | 6–9 months full-time / 10–16 part-time |
| **VS-A** (single-player, **the shippable fallback**) | Outer ring of the web map; one procgen room kit | Procgen derelicts; 2nd horror type; all 4 hallucination classes with falsification checks; one derelict kit at target HD-pixel fidelity under the lighting model | +8–12 months |
| **VS-B** (co-op) | Same content | 2-player LAN listen-server; authority model proven with two local instances | +4–6 months, only after VS-A is complete |
| **Alpha** | 3 depth rings; full kit set; lore fragments | Steam lobbies / NAT; crew scars and knowledge persistence (failure contract); versioned saves; host-owned world + guest carry-over; true-value debug overlay | +12–18 months |
| **Full Vision** | Early Access launch | Polish; adaptive audio; accessibility; onboarding | ~4–6 years total |

**What ships if time runs out**: VS-A, as a small single-player survival-horror
game. Co-op and depth rings are cut; the product is whole.

# Art Bible


## Phase 0: Parse Arguments and Context Check


See `.claude/docs/director-gates.md` for the full check pattern. Individual gate definitions live in `.claude/docs/director-gates/[gate-id].md` — the spawned agent reads its own gate file; do not read it in the parent session.


Every `AskUserQuestion` call follows `.claude/docs/automation-modes.md`
(collaborative asks always · guided major-only · autonomous logs and proceeds;
`automation_always_ask` categories always prompt).

**`docs.density`** — it controls per-section *depth*, where `workflow`
controls which sections exist. `modes.rigor` sets both together; set
`docs.density` explicitly to vary depth alone: `terse` (the default, via `rigor: minimal`) = each section a bulleted list of
constraints + references; `balanced` = paragraphs explaining each visual choice
(`rigor: standard`); `thorough` = full prose including style explorations, references, and
rationale per choice. Apply it to every section you author.

**`workflow`** (see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`):
- `full` — all 9 art bible sections required.
- `standard` — required only if visual asset stories exist in the project;
  sections 1–4 are the minimum when required. `workflow_overrides.art_bible_strict:
  true` forces all 9 sections regardless of tier.
- `minimal` — not required. Can still be run voluntarily.

Read `design/gdd/game-concept.md` — or `design/game-brief.md`, the one-page brief
that replaces it at `rigor: minimal`. If neither exists, fail with:
> "No game concept found. Run `/brainstorm` first — the art bible is authored after the game concept is approved."

Extract from game-concept.md (from the brief: working title, pitch, "Who it's for /
what they feel" line and "Art & audio direction" line — it has no pillars, Visual
Identity Anchor or platform):
- Game title (working title)
- Core fantasy and elevator pitch
- Game pillars (all of them)
- **Visual Identity Anchor** section if present (from brainstorm Phase 4 art-director output)
- Target platform (if noted)

**Retrofit mode detection**: Glob `design/art/art-bible.md`. If the file exists,
build the status table **without reading the document** — you are about to author
only the *incomplete* sections, so loading the complete ones is loading exactly
what you will not touch:

```
Grep pattern="^## " path="design/art/art-bible.md" output_mode="content" -n
Grep pattern="\[To be designed\]|\[TBD\]|\[To be written\]|^_?TODO" path="design/art/art-bible.md" output_mode="content" -n
```

- The first grep gives the section headings and their line numbers — the gap
  between consecutive headings is that section's size.
- The second gives placeholder markers and where they fall.
- A section is **Complete** if it has substantive distance to the next heading and
  no placeholder marker inside it; **Placeholder** if a marker falls in its range;
  **Empty** if consecutive headings sit adjacent.
- Where the two greps leave a section genuinely ambiguous, read *that section's*
  line range with `Read(offset, limit)` — never the whole file.
- Build a section status table:

```
Section | Status
--------|--------
1. Visual Identity Statement | [Complete / Empty / Placeholder]
2. Mood & Atmosphere | ...
3. Shape Language | ...
4. Color System | ...
5. Character Design Direction | ...
6. Environment Design Language | ...
7. UI/HUD Visual Direction | ...
8. Asset Standards | ...
9. Reference Direction | ...
```

- Present this table to the user:
  > "Found existing art bible at `design/art/art-bible.md`. [N] sections are complete, [M] need content. I'll work on the incomplete sections only — existing content will not be touched."
- Only work on sections with Status: Empty or Placeholder. Do not re-author sections that are already complete.

If the file does not exist, this is a fresh authoring session. The first
approved section creates the file from `.claude/docs/templates/art-bible.md`,
whose nine `## N. Name` headings are the ones retrofit mode reads — ask first:
"May I create `design/art/art-bible.md` from the art bible template?" Each
approved section then replaces its own `[To be designed]` line with `Edit`;
keep the headings as the template has them.

**A section's approval names its write.** Every section is approved through an
`AskUserQuestion` whose approving option is `[A] Lock this in and write it to
design/art/art-bible.md` (Section 1's full option list is below). Choosing it is
the approval to write that section; no section is written without it, fresh or
retrofit.

Extract performance budgets and the engine for asset standard constraints: read `performance.*` and `engine.name` from `project.yaml`; for any key absent or empty (including when `project.yaml` has no `performance` or `engine` block), fall back to `.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md`.

---

## Phase 1: Framing

Present the session context and ask two questions before authoring anything:

Use `AskUserQuestion` with two tabs:
- Tab **"Scope"** — "Which sections need to be authored today?"
  Options: `Full bible — all 9 sections` / `Visual identity core (sections 1–4 only)` / `Asset standards only (section 8)` / `Resume — fill in missing sections`

  **Mark the option the resolved `workflow` tier actually requires as
  (Recommended), and say why** — the tier already decides this and the user
  should not have to know the tier table to answer:
  - `full` → **Full bible** — all 9 sections are required at this tier.
  - `standard` → **Visual identity core (sections 1–4 only)** — that is the
    documented minimum when an art bible is required at all. Say: "Sections 1–4
    are what `standard` requires; 5–9 are available if you want them."
  - `minimal` → no art bible is required. Say so before asking, and offer
    sections 1–4 as the useful-if-you-want-it option rather than defaulting to 9.
  - `workflow_overrides.art_bible_strict: true` → **Full bible** regardless of tier.

  This is the single biggest cost lever in this skill: every authored section
  carries a specialist spawn, so authoring 9 sections where the tier requires 4
  more than doubles the run for artifacts nothing downstream will check.
- Tab **"References"** — "Do you have reference games, films, or art that define the visual direction?"
  (Free text — let the user type specific titles. Do NOT preset options here.)

If the game-concept.md has a Visual Identity Anchor section, note it:
> "Found a visual identity anchor from brainstorm: '[anchor name] — [one-line rule]'. I'll use this as the foundation for the art bible."

**Author only the sections in the chosen scope.** Phases 2–4 run only the
sections inside it — for `Resume`, the Empty and Placeholder rows of the
retrofit table — and skip every other section, and any phase left with none.
Phase 6 names each section not authored this run and why.

---

## Phase 2: Visual Identity Foundation (Sections 1–4)

These four sections define the core visual language. **All other sections flow from them.** Author and write each to file before moving to the next.

> **Spawn policy for this phase.** Section 1 is delegated on its own — it is
> foundational and the user chooses between anchor directions before anything
> else can build on it. Sections 2–4 are then delegated in **one** `art-director`
> call, not three: they are the same agent receiving the same inputs (Visual
> Identity Statement + pillars), and mood, shape and colour are interdependent —
> an art director defines them together, not in isolation. Three separate calls
> re-sent the same context three times and asked the agent to reason about
> colour without knowing the shape language it had just written.
>
> **This is not reduced specialist involvement** — every section is still
> authored by the specialist, which is the point `.claude/docs/effects-map.md`
> makes about art-bible delegation being mandatory. It is one call instead of
> three for the same three sections. Per-section user approval and
> write-to-file-immediately are unchanged.

### Section 1: Visual Identity Statement

**Goal**: A one-line visual rule plus 2–3 supporting principles that resolve visual ambiguity.

If a visual anchor exists from game-concept.md: present it and ask:
- "Build directly from this anchor?"
- "Revise it before expanding?"
- "Start fresh with new options?"

**Agent delegation (MANDATORY)**: Spawn `art-director` via `Agent`:
- Provide: game concept (elevator pitch, core fantasy), full pillar set, platform target, any reference games/art from Phase 1 framing, the visual anchor if it exists
- Ask: "Draft a Visual Identity Statement for this game. Provide: (1) a one-line visual rule that could resolve any visual decision ambiguity, (2) 2–3 supporting visual principles, each with a one-sentence design test ('when X is ambiguous, this principle says choose Y'). Anchor all principles directly in the stated pillars — each principle must serve a specific pillar. (From a one-page brief, which has no pillars, anchor them in its pitch and "what they feel" line.)"

Present the art-director's draft to the user. Use `AskUserQuestion`:
- Options: `[A] Lock this in and write it to design/art/art-bible.md` / `[B] Revise the one-liner` / `[C] Revise a supporting principle` / `[D] Describe my own direction`

Write the approved section to file immediately.

### Section 2: Mood & Atmosphere

**Goal**: Emotional targets by game state — specific enough for a lighting artist to work from.

For each major game state (e.g., exploration, combat, victory, defeat, menus — adapt to this game's states), define:
- Primary emotion/mood target
- Lighting character (time of day, color temperature, contrast level)
- Atmospheric descriptors (3–5 adjectives)
- Energy level (frenetic / measured / contemplative / etc.)

**Agent delegation for Sections 2–4 — one call, issued here.** Spawn
`art-director` via `Agent` with the locked Visual Identity Statement and pillar set,
and ask for all three sections in a single brief:

1. **Mood & atmosphere** — "Define mood and atmosphere targets for each major game state in this game. Be specific — 'dark and foreboding' is not enough. Name the exact emotional target, the lighting character (warm/cool, high/low contrast, time of day direction), and at least one visual element that carries the mood. Each game state must feel visually distinct from the others."
2. **Shape language** — "Define the shape language for this game. Connect each shape principle back to the visual identity statement and a specific game pillar. Explain what these shape choices communicate to the player emotionally."
3. **Colour system** — "Design the color system for this game. Every semantic color assignment must be explained — why does this color mean danger/safety/reward in this world? Identify which color pairs might fail colorblind players and specify what backup cues are needed."

Require the three to be **mutually consistent** — the palette must serve the mood
targets and the shape hierarchy — and returned as three separately labelled
blocks so each can be approved and written on its own.

Then present **Section 2** to the user, approve it, and write it to file
immediately before moving to Section 3. Do not present all three at once: the
batching is in the delegation, not in the review.

### Section 3: Shape Language

**Goal**: The geometric vocabulary that makes this game's world visually coherent and distinguishable.

Cover:
- Character silhouette philosophy (how readable at thumbnail size? Distinguishing trait per archetype?)
- Environment geometry (angular/curved/organic/geometric — which dominates and why?)
- UI shape grammar (does UI echo the world aesthetic, or is it a distinct HUD language?)
- Hero shapes vs. supporting shapes (what draws the eye, what recedes?)

**Draft source**: the Sections 2–4 delegation issued under Section 2 — use the
shape-language block it returned. Do not spawn again.

Write the approved section to file immediately.

### Section 4: Color System

**Goal**: A complete, producible palette system that serves both aesthetic and communication needs.

Cover:
- Primary palette (5–7 colors with roles — not just hex codes, but what each color means in this world)
- Semantic color usage (what does red communicate? Gold? Blue? White? Establish the color vocabulary)
- Per-biome or per-area color temperature rules (if the game has distinct areas)
- UI palette (may differ from world palette — define the divergence explicitly)
- Colorblind safety: which semantic colors need shape/icon/sound backup

**Draft source**: the Sections 2–4 delegation issued under Section 2 — use the
colour-system block it returned. Do not spawn again.

Write the approved section to file immediately.

---

## Phase 3: Production Guides (Sections 5–8)

These sections translate the visual identity into concrete production rules. They should be specific enough that an outsourcing team can follow them without additional briefing.

### Section 5: Character Design Direction

**Agent delegation for Sections 5–6 — one call, issued here.** Both sections
were separate spawns of the **same agent with the same input** (`sections 1–4`),
which is pure duplication: the second call re-sent the whole visual identity to
an agent that had just been given it. Spawn `art-director` once with sections
1–4 and ask for both:

1. **Character design direction** — "Cover: visual archetype for the player character (if any), distinguishing feature rules per character type (how do players tell enemies/NPCs/allies apart at a glance?), expression/pose style targets (stiff/expressive/realistic/exaggerated), and LOD philosophy (how much detail is preserved at game camera distance?)."
2. **Environment design language** — "Cover: architectural style and its relationship to the world's culture/history, texture philosophy (painted vs. PBR vs. stylized — why this choice for this game?), prop density rules (sparse/dense — what drives the choice per area type?), and environmental storytelling guidelines (what visual details should tell the story without text?)."

Require characters and environments to be **legible against each other** — a
character silhouette must read against the environment texture density the same
brief defines. Return two separately labelled blocks.

Present **Section 5** first, approve, write to file, then Section 6.

### Section 6: Environment Design Language

**Draft source**: the Sections 5–6 delegation issued under Section 5 — use the
environment block it returned. Do not spawn again.

Write the approved section to file.

### Section 7: UI/HUD Visual Direction

**Agent delegation**: Spawn in parallel:
- **`art-director`**: Visual style for UI — diegetic vs. screen-space HUD, typography direction (font personality, weight, size hierarchy), iconography style (flat/outlined/illustrated/photorealistic), animation feel for UI elements
- **`ux-designer`**: UX alignment check — does the visual direction support the interaction patterns this game requires? Flag any conflicts between art direction and readability/accessibility needs.

Collect both. If they conflict (e.g., art-director wants elaborate diegetic UI but ux-designer flags it would reduce combat readability), surface the conflict explicitly with both positions. Do NOT silently resolve — use `AskUserQuestion` to let the user decide.

Write the approved section to file.

### Section 8: Asset Standards

**Agent delegation**: Spawn in parallel:
- **`art-director`**: File format preferences, naming convention direction, texture resolution tiers, LOD level expectations, export settings philosophy
- **`technical-artist`**: Engine-specific hard constraints — poly count budgets per asset category, texture memory limits, material slot counts, importer constraints, anything from the performance budgets (`performance.*` in `project.yaml`, falling back to `.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md`)

If any art preference conflicts with a technical constraint (e.g., art-director wants 4K textures but performance budget requires 2K for mobile), surface the conflict explicitly with both positions — the ideal and the constrained standard, and the tradeoff. Do NOT silently resolve it — use `AskUserQuestion` to let the user pick (options: the ideal standard, the constrained standard, or document both and let per-asset judgment apply). Ambiguity in asset standards is where production costs are born.

Write the approved section to file.

---

## Phase 4: Reference Direction (Section 9)

**Goal**: A curated reference set that is specific about what to take and what to avoid from each source.

**Agent delegation**: Spawn `art-director` via `Agent` with the completed sections 1–8. Ask: "Compile a reference direction for this game. Provide 3–5 reference sources (games, films, art styles, or specific artists). For each: name it, specify exactly what visual element to draw from it (not 'the general aesthetic' — a specific technique, color choice, or compositional rule), and specify what to explicitly avoid or diverge from (to prevent the 'trying to copy X' reading). References should be additive — no two references should be pointing in exactly the same direction."

Write the approved section to file.

---

## Phase 5: Art Director Sign-Off

**Review mode check** — apply before spawning AD-ART-BIBLE:
- `solo` → skip. Note: "AD-ART-BIBLE skipped — Solo mode." Then record the skip
  (below) and proceed to Phase 6.
- `lean` → skip (not a PHASE-GATE). Note: "AD-ART-BIBLE skipped — Lean mode."
  Then record the skip (below) and proceed to Phase 6.
- `full` → spawn as normal.

On either skip, ask "May I record the skipped sign-off in
`design/art/art-bible.md`'s header?" and, on yes, replace the header's
`> **Art Director Sign-Off (AD-ART-BIBLE)**: [Not yet reviewed]` with
`> **Art Director Sign-Off (AD-ART-BIBLE)**: SKIPPED [date] — [solo|lean] mode`
— the gate accepts either form as a recorded sign-off.

After all sections are complete (or the scoped set from Phase 1 is complete), spawn `art-director` via `Agent` using gate **AD-ART-BIBLE** (`.claude/docs/director-gates/ad-art-bible.md`).

Pass: the art bible path (`design/art/art-bible.md`); the game pillars and core
fantasy; the platform and performance constraints (`platform.*` and
`performance.*` from `project.yaml`, falling back to
`.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md`); and the visual identity anchor. When
Phase 0 read the one-page brief, pass its pitch and "what they feel" line as the
pillars and fantasy, and its "Art & audio direction" line as the anchor.

Handle verdict per standard rules in `director-gates.md`.
On `Revise flagged items`, or to resolve a REJECT, the section's own specialist
— `art-director`, with `ux-designer` for Section 7 and `technical-artist` for
Section 8 — re-drafts each flagged section, which is then presented, approved
and written like any other section before `REVISED [date]` is recorded.
A `NOT ASSESSED` answer is never an approval: name the missing input, then
supply it and re-run the gate, or record `NOT ASSESSED`.
Record the verdict in the art bible's status header:
`> **Art Director Sign-Off (AD-ART-BIBLE)**: APPROVED [date] / CONCERNS (accepted) [date] / REVISED [date] / NOT ASSESSED [date] — [missing input]`

---

## Phase 6: Close

First, name each of the nine sections not authored this run and why — outside
the chosen scope, or already complete — e.g. *"Not authored this run: sections
5–9 (outside the chosen scope; `standard` requires 1–4)."* A run that stopped
after Section 4 must not read like a finished bible.

Before presenting next steps, check project state:
- Does `design/gdd/systems-index.md` exist? → map-systems is done, skip that option
- Is an engine configured — `engine.name` present in `project.yaml`, or a configured Engine field (not `[TO BE CONFIGURED]`) in `.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md`? → setup-engine is done, skip that option
- Does `design/gdd/` contain any `*.md` files? → design-system has been run, skip that option
- Does `design/gdd/gdd-cross-review-*.md` exist? → review-all-gdds is done
- Do GDDs exist (check above)? → include /consistency-check option

Use `AskUserQuestion` for next steps. Only include options that are genuinely next based on the state check above:

At `workflow: minimal`, the pool is `/create-stories` (no stories yet) or
`/dev-story [next story]`, plus Stop here — the GDD/architecture pool below is
`standard`/`full` only.

**Option pool — include only if not already done:**
- `[_] Run /map-systems — decompose the concept into systems before writing GDDs` (skip if systems-index.md exists)
- `[_] Run /setup-engine — configure the engine (asset standards may need revisiting after engine is set)` (skip if engine configured)
- `[_] Run /design-system — start the first GDD` (skip if any GDDs exist)
- `[_] Run /review-all-gdds — cross-GDD consistency check (required before Technical Setup gate)` (skip if gdd-cross-review-*.md exists)
- `[_] Run /asset-spec — generate per-asset visual specs and AI generation prompts from approved GDDs` (include if GDDs exist)
- `[_] Run /consistency-check — scan existing GDDs against the art bible for visual direction conflicts` (include if GDDs exist)
- `[_] Run /create-architecture — author the master architecture document (next Technical Setup step)`
- `[_] Stop here`

Assign letters A, B, C… only to the options actually included. Mark the most logical pipeline-advancing option as `(recommended)`.

> **Always include** (`standard`/`full` only) `/create-architecture` and Stop here as options — these are always valid next steps once the art bible is complete.

---

## Collaborative Protocol

**Applies in `collaborative` mode (the default).** For `guided` and
`autonomous` modes, see `.claude/docs/automation-modes.md` — the rules below
describe what collaborative mode requires, not universal behavior.

Every section follows: **Question → Options → Decision → Draft (from art-director agent) → Approval → Write to file**

- Never draft a section yourself — every section's content comes from the
  relevant specialist. One delegation may cover several sections (2–4 share a
  call, as do 5–6), but no section may be written from the orchestrator's own
  judgement instead of an agent's.
- Write each section to file immediately after approval — do not batch **the
  writes or the approvals**. Batching applies only to the delegation call; the
  user still sees, approves and commits one section at a time.
- Surface all agent disagreements to the user — never silently resolve conflicts between art-director and technical-artist
- The art bible is a constraint document: it restricts future decisions in exchange for visual coherence. Every section should feel like it narrows the solution space productively.

---

> **Status**: [Draft / Under Review / Approved]
> **Owned By**: art-director
> **Last Updated**: [Date]
> **Art Director Sign-Off (AD-ART-BIBLE)**: [Not yet reviewed]

`/art-bible` writes these nine sections in this order and replaces each
section's `[To be designed]` line as that section is approved. A section still
holding its placeholder is incomplete; a later run fills only those.

## 1. Visual Identity Statement

[To be designed] — a one-line visual rule that resolves any visual ambiguity,
plus 2–3 supporting principles, each with a design test ("when X is ambiguous,
choose Y") and the pillar it serves.

## 2. Mood & Atmosphere

[To be designed] — for each major game state (exploration, combat, victory,
defeat, menus — whichever this game has): the emotional target, lighting
character (time of day, colour temperature, contrast), 3–5 atmospheric
descriptors, and energy level. Each state must look distinct from the others.

## 3. Shape Language

[To be designed] — character silhouette philosophy (readable at thumbnail
size, one distinguishing trait per archetype), environment geometry, UI shape
grammar, and hero versus supporting shapes.

## 4. Color System

[To be designed] — a primary palette of 5–7 colours with their meaning in this
world, semantic colour usage, per-area colour temperature rules, the UI palette
and where it diverges, and colourblind safety: which semantic colours need a
shape, icon or sound backup.

## 5. Character Design Direction

[To be designed] — the player character's visual archetype, how players tell
enemies, NPCs and allies apart at a glance, expression and pose style, and how
much detail survives at game camera distance (LOD philosophy).

## 6. Environment Design Language

[To be designed] — architectural style and its tie to the world's culture,
texture philosophy (painted, PBR or stylised, and why), prop density rules per
area type, and environmental storytelling guidelines.

## 7. UI/HUD Visual Direction

[To be designed] — diegetic versus screen-space HUD, typography (personality,
weight, size hierarchy, minimum readable size), iconography style, UI animation
feel, and any art-direction versus readability conflict and how it was decided.

## 8. Asset Standards

[To be designed] — file formats, naming convention, texture resolution tiers,
LOD levels, export settings, and the engine's hard limits (poly budgets per
asset category, texture memory, material slots). Where an art preference and a
technical limit disagree, record both and the trade-off chosen.

## 9. Reference Direction

[To be designed] — 3–5 references (games, films, art styles or artists). For
each: the specific element to take from it, and what to avoid so the result
does not read as a copy.
---

  **Direction: *What You Light, You Can Read***
  
  ### The Rule
  
  > **Light is a resource you spend. Inside it, every machine states its condition. Outside it, the dark is honest.**
  
  **How to use it.** When two visual choices both seem fine, ask three questions in order. The first answer that separates them decides the choice.
  1. Does one of them make the player *spend* something (light, power, attention) to learn what they see?
  2. Does one of them put the information *in the world* (a moving part, a medium, a trail) instead of on top of it?

  **Alternatives considered.**
  - *"The Dark Is the Default"* alone. It gives strong mood but nothing to say about how a lit machine should look, so it would leave the Satisfactory-style legibility to chance.
  - *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).
  - The hybrid keeps both. Legibility is the reward and darkness is the price.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 1: Darkness Is Honest; Light Is a Decision
  **Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).
  
  Rooms are not fogged, they are *unlit*. Geometry always exists, and any source reveals it exactly as it is. The visible-world edge is the real edge of a real light, never a mask. The physical radius your light actually reveals is a fixed anchor and never lies. Even at low sanity, the hallucination layer may add things but may not move that boundary.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 1 says the physical world is ground truth and only instruments and perception can be wrong. A vignette or fog-of-war mask is an interface lying about the world, and it would give the sanity system nothing to betray. True occlusion gives the player a reliable baseline. A hallucinated shadow with no occluder is then frightening *because* occlusion is normally trustworthy. It also makes light a decision, since each lamp is a visible cost with a visible reach.
  
  **Design test.** When a vignette or fog-of-war mask competes with true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff, choose the true occlusion.
  
  **Alternative rejected.** A soft ambient-reveal radius around the player. It is cheaper to build and reads well, but it makes the player the light source for free, which erases the spend-light economy.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 2: Inside the Light, State Lives in the Sprite, Not the Icon
  **Serves Pillar 2, Dread Before Chaos** (and Pillar 1, since the physical world carries the truth).
  
  Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (a rotor, a fluid, a filament). Failure renders as a trail in the loop's own hue: puddle, frost, scorch, mist, drip. A trail is also a tell. Every breach is preceded by a perceivable escalation, and that escalation is drawn *in the world*, so a careful player can read it. Hue coding is always redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) so it stays readable for colorblind players.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 2 needs tells a careful player could have caught. A banner is read once and dismissed, but a frosting elbow can be seen to worsen from across the room. This is the Satisfactory lesson: watching a machine work is its own reward, and failure can be diagnosed by following the eye along the pipe. Resource loops keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O2 cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey), so a hue is a vocabulary the player learns once.
  
  **Design test.** When a status LED or a "COOLANT LOW" banner competes with a turning rotor with visible fluid or a frosted elbow with a drip, choose the rotor and the elbow.
  
  **Alternatives rejected.**
  - A world-space icon layer on every system. It is cheap, but it reads as an interface and it gives the hallucination system an easy, un-physical target.
  - Heavy per-state sprite sets. They are too expensive for a solo developer, so state should come from shared hue, trail and motion systems instead.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 3: Emission Is Exposure
  **Serves Pillar 3, The Web Watches.**
  
  Running loops glow in their own hue. With power off, the ship is lit only by what is still running. Every loop you run is a lantern the web can see. The web itself has no hue of its own and appears only in your light, as oily iridescence under direct illumination. Deeper rings do not change hue. They lower ambient light and raise the iridescence.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 3 says Attention is shown in the world, never as a hidden meter, and that restraint is a real strategy. Making light, power use and visibility the *same thing visually* means going dark is a legible tactical choice, not a menu setting. Tying the web's appearance to the player's own light also makes the web's presence feel like a consequence of the player's choices, which supports the "dread is feeling it come" hinge. Keeping hue constant across depth keeps the loop vocabulary from Principle 2 reliable at every ring. Depth is expressed only through ambient and iridescence.
  
  **Design test.** When an on-screen attention meter competes with more filaments resolving in the player's light cone as Attention rises, choose the filaments.
  
  **Alternative rejected.** Shifting the palette per depth ring. It gives strong depth identity, but it would break the flow-coded hue vocabulary, and it would compete with the violet and flesh-tone rule below.
  
  ---
  
  ### Corollary: When the Game Lies, the Lie Leaks (serves Pillar 4)
  
  This is a binding constraint on Pillar 4's hallucination classes, not a fourth principle.
  
  - **Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world.** When either appears, it is the player's sanity and never the location. Every hallucination leaks them somewhere: a fringe, a flicker, a tint at the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
  - **Drift order.** Instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the ship), then the light lies (the cone seems to reach further than it does, shadows with no occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at pipe edges and flesh tones enter.

  **Design test.** When a hallucination is perfectly seamless and a hallucination leaks the sane palette, choose the leak.
  
  ---
  
  ### Constraint Notes
  
  - **Art style.** HD pixel art at 3/4 oblique top-down, with Godot 4.7.2 2D lighting. Readability under light comes from silhouette, hue and motion, not from texture noise. This keeps sprites cheap to author and keeps the lighting doing the visual work.

  - **Open for the technical artist.** Whether true occlusion at hard falloff, many emissive loops, and a per-client hallucination filter all fit the lighting budget is unmeasured. If they don't, the first thing to cut is the number of simultaneous emitters, not the occlusion rule in Principle 1.
  
  ### Reference Touchstones
  
  - **Project Zomboid.** Lived-in detail and a dark world that you move through at a patient pace.
  - **Satisfactory.** Legible machinery and flows you can read at a glance.
  - **Stellaris.** Dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes.

  - **Beyond the Aquila Rift.** A kind-looking lie, where the wrongness is in what leaks through.
  - **Pandorum.** Waking into wrongness aboard a derelict.
  
  ### Checklist
  
  For any new asset or visual feature, answer these before approval.
  1. Does it make the player spend light to see it (Principle 1)?
  2. Does its state live in a moving part or a trail, not an icon (Principle 2)?
  3. If it glows, is that glow exposure, and does it carry the right hue (Principle 3)?
  4. Does it avoid violet and flesh tones in the sane world (Corollary)?
  5. If it is an anchor (character sprite, hand tool, HUD frame, light radius), does it stay unshifted under hallucination (Corollary)?

> **Light is a resource you spend. Inside it, every machine states its condition. Outside it, the dark is honest.**

**How to use it.** When two visual choices both seem fine, ask three questions in order. The first answer that separates them decides the choice.
1. Does one of them make the player *spend* something (light, power, attention) to learn what they see?
2. Does one of them put the information *in the world* (a moving part, a medium, a trail) instead of on top of it?
3. If the player is lied to here, will the lie leak the sane palette?

**Why this works as a tie-breaker.** It is one sentence with three clauses that map to three kinds of decision: lighting, state display, and truth. Almost every art question lands in one of those. It also keeps the art workload honest. The main cost sits in the 2D lighting pipeline rather than in sprite-state count, so the rule favors cheap, systemic answers (a light, a hue, a trail) over expensive bespoke ones (a new animation per state).

**Alternatives considered.**
- *"The Dark Is the Default"* alone. It gives strong mood but nothing to say about how a lit machine should look, so it would leave the Satisfactory-style legibility to chance.
- *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).
- The hybrid keeps both. Legibility is the reward and darkness is the price.

### Principle 1: Darkness Is Honest; Light Is a Decision
**Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).

Rooms are not fogged, they are *unlit*. Geometry always exists, and any source reveals it exactly as it is. The visible-world edge is the real edge of a real light, never a mask. The physical radius your light actually reveals is a fixed anchor and never lies. Even at low sanity, the hallucination layer may add things but may not move that boundary.

**Rationale.** Pillar 1 says the physical world is ground truth and only instruments and perception can be wrong. A vignette or fog-of-war mask is an interface lying about the world, and it would give the sanity system nothing to betray. True occlusion gives the player a reliable baseline. A hallucinated shadow with no occluder is then frightening *because* occlusion is normally trustworthy. It also makes light a decision, since each lamp is a visible cost with a visible reach.

**Design test.** When a vignette or fog-of-war mask competes with true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff, choose the true occlusion.

**Alternative rejected.** A soft ambient-reveal radius around the player. It is cheaper to build and reads well, but it makes the player the light source for free, which erases the spend-light economy.

### Principle 2: Inside the Light, State Lives in the Sprite, Not the Icon
**Serves Pillar 2, Dread Before Chaos** (and Pillar 1, since the physical world carries the truth).

Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (a rotor, a fluid, a filament). Failure renders as a trail in the loop's own hue: puddle, frost, scorch, mist, drip. A trail is also a tell. Every breach is preceded by a perceivable escalation, and that escalation is drawn *in the world*, so a careful player can read it. Hue coding is always redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) so it stays readable for colorblind players.

**Rationale.** Pillar 2 needs tells a careful player could have caught. A banner is read once and dismissed, but a frosting elbow can be seen to worsen from across the room. This is the Satisfactory lesson: watching a machine work is its own reward, and failure can be diagnosed by following the eye along the pipe. Resource loops keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O₂ cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey), so a hue is a vocabulary the player learns once.

**Design test.** When a status LED or a "COOLANT LOW" banner competes with a turning rotor with visible fluid or a frosted elbow with a drip, choose the rotor and the elbow.

**Alternatives rejected.**
- A world-space icon layer on every system. It is cheap, but it reads as an interface and it gives the hallucination system an easy, un-physical target.
- Heavy per-state sprite sets. They are too expensive for a solo developer, so state should come from shared hue, trail and motion systems instead.

### Principle 3: Emission Is Exposure
**Serves Pillar 3, The Web Watches.**

Running loops glow in their own hue. With power off, the ship is lit only by what is still running. Every loop you run is a lantern the web can see. The web itself has no hue of its own and appears only in your light, as oily iridescence under direct illumination. Deeper rings do not change hue. They lower ambient light and raise the iridescence.

**Rationale.** Pillar 3 says Attention is shown in the world, never as a hidden meter, and that restraint is a real strategy. Making light, power use and visibility the *same thing visually* means going dark is a legible tactical choice, not a menu setting. Tying the web's appearance to the player's own light also makes the web's presence feel like a consequence of the player's choices, which supports the "dread is feeling it come" hinge. Keeping hue constant across depth keeps the loop vocabulary from Principle 2 reliable at every ring. Depth is expressed only through ambient and iridescence.

**Design test.** When an on-screen attention meter competes with more filaments resolving in the player's light cone as Attention rises, choose the filaments.

**Alternative rejected.** Shifting the palette per depth ring. It gives strong depth identity, but it would break the flow-coded hue vocabulary, and it would compete with the violet and flesh-tone rule below.

### Corollary: When the Game Lies, the Lie Leaks (serves Pillar 4)

This is a binding constraint on Pillar 4's hallucination classes, not a fourth principle.

- **Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world.** When either appears, it is the player's sanity and never the location. Every hallucination leaks them somewhere: a fringe, a flicker, a tint at the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
- **Drift order.** Instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the ship), then the light lies (the cone seems to reach further than it does, shadows with no occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at pipe edges and flesh tones enter.
- **Anchors that never shift.** Character sprites, hand tools, the HUD frame, and the true light radius. A crewmate's own light beam (colour and shape) also stays truthful, per Pillar 1's human channel.

**Design test.** A seamless hallucination vs. one that leaks the sane palette → the leak.

### Constraint Notes

- **Art style.** HD pixel art at 3/4 oblique top-down, with Godot 4.7.2 2D lighting. Readability under light comes from silhouette, hue and motion, not from texture noise. This keeps sprites cheap to author and keeps the lighting doing the visual work.
- **Pipeline consequence.** The lighting-budget spike (a lighting test on D3D12) is the *first* spike, because all three principles depend on 2D lights, occlusion and emission being affordable.
- **Open for the technical artist.** Whether true occlusion at hard falloff, many emissive loops, and a per-client hallucination filter all fit the lighting budget is unmeasured. If they don't, the first thing to cut is the number of simultaneous emitters, not the occlusion rule in Principle 1.

### Reference Touchstones

- **Project Zomboid.** Lived-in detail and a dark world that you move through at a patient pace.
- **Satisfactory.** Legible machinery and flows you can read at a glance.
- **Stellaris.** Dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes.
- **Barotrauma.** A 2D hostile vessel, with failure you can see happening.
- **Beyond the Aquila Rift.** A kind-looking lie, where the wrongness is in what leaks through.
- **Pandorum.** Waking into wrongness aboard a derelict.

### Checklist

For any new asset or visual feature, answer these before approval.
1. Does it make the player spend light to see it (Principle 1)?
2. Does its state live in a moving part or a trail, not an icon (Principle 2)?
3. If it glows, is that glow exposure, and does it carry the right hue (Principle 3)?
4. Does it avoid violet and flesh tones in the sane world (Corollary)?
5. If it is an anchor (character sprite, hand tool, HUD frame, light radius), does it stay unshifted under hallucination (Corollary)?

  ### 7.0 Governing rule: the HUD is a suit, the ship is an instrument

  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | **In-world instruments** | the ship, the pod, a derelict | sprites in the world layer: gauges, sight-glasses, dials on panels, the pod dash, the chart-table console | yes — unreadable until lit | yes; this is class (b)'s primary home ("from the gauge to the sprite") | the instrument housing is physical geometry (P1); its reading is not |

  | **Chart table (meta)** | nobody in the fiction: keybinds, menus, settings, the web map | screen-space, 2.11 register | no | **never** — it is not an instrument | whole layer is honest by definition |

Nothing else. In particular:
  
  - **No sanity meter and no attention meter.** Principle 3's design test and 4.6 already forbid them; the only sanity that reaches screen-space is the violet gleam on a *reading* that is lying. Attention lives in the filaments at the cone edge (2.7). A player who wants to know how watched they are must look at the world, which is the game.
  - **No ship state on the suit layer.** "COOLANT LOW" is the banner Principle 2 rejected. The ship tells you its state along its pipes; the suit tells you about you.
  - **No minimap in play.** A minimap is a vignette-free fog-of-war mask drawn small (Principle 1's rejected alternative). The web map (7.4) is a chart you open, not a radar you glance at.

It is drawn on the HUD layer in the chart-table register, anchored to the object's screen position, and **is drawn only when the object is inside the lit area** (the technical-artist sets the illumination threshold). Nothing is prompted in the dark, so the prompt teaches the rule rather than breaking it. When the player needs precision they *inspect* the instrument: a screen-space magnification of that same gauge, framed by the ship's own bezel dialect, with numerals in the reading register. Two rules: the inspect view is drawn only for an instrument that is currently lit (whether inspection is *permitted* unlit is the game-designer's; visually there is nothing to magnify), and the inspect view is **the same instrument**, not a second one — it lies exactly when the gauge on the wall lies, gleam included. Pillar 4's "second instrument" check is a *different* gauge elsewhere on the ship, never the zoom.
  
  **Composition.** The beam cone is the brightest shape in frame and the eye's home (3.5). The HUD must therefore stay at the edges, small and cool.   ### 7.1 Typography
  
  **Personality: stamped nameplate and engraved dial.** Industrial, humanist, un-ornamented, slightly condensed.   | Face | Used for | Why this face |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Instrument face** — a bitmap pixel font on the art grid | suit readings, frame labels, in-world instrument numerals in the inspect view, keybind glyphs, map labels | the HUD is the ship's dialect (3.4) and must sit on the same pixel grid as the ship; an antialiased vector glyph beside a pixel bezel reads as a browser overlay, and the integer grid makes a needle's one-pixel wander legible (7.3) |

  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Reading numerals | suit O₂ value, inspect view, map distance | ≥ 21 | ≥ 28 | 7 |
  | Label | gauge names, hand-rail tool names, crew names | ≥ 15 | ≥ 20 | 5 |
  | Caption floor | the smallest glyph anywhere | 15 | 20 | 5 |
  | Menu body (reading face) | settings, logs | ≥ 20 px font size | ≥ 26 | — |
  | Lore long-form | recovered logs read in full | ≥ 22 | ≥ 29 | — |
  | Section heading | menu groups | ≥ 24 | ≥ 32 | — |
  | Title | screen names | ≥ 32 | ≥ 42 | — |

The frame grows with the integer step; the beam does not, so a player who scales the HUD up spends some of the frame area the beam would otherwise own — that is their accessibility trade, made explicit.
  
  **Alternatives considered.**
  - *One pixel font everywhere.* Rejected — lore and settings become hard to read, and every accessibility size step is an integer jump.
  - *One vector font everywhere.* Rejected — a smooth face on pixel bezels breaks "the HUD is the home-ship's dialect" (3.4), and sub-pixel glyph edges make a one-pixel needle wander invisible.
  - *A pixel font with several hand-drawn sizes.* Viable but costly for a solo developer; revisit only if the two-face split fails a readability test.
  
  ### 7.2 Iconography
  
  **Flat silhouettes, one colour, on the art grid.** No outlines, no gradients, no illustration, no drop shadows. A flat stamped silhouette is what a plate on this ship would carry; an outlined icon adds a second line colour and reads as web UI; an illustrated icon is a picture of a thing rather than the thing's grammar.
  
  **Icons are the fitting table.** Per 3.4, loop glyphs are the loop's fitting silhouette plus its flow mark, so shape carries meaning with hue removed (4.7):
  
  | Loop | Glyph | Flow mark inside the glyph |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | O₂ | thin ring clamp | three close-pitched chevrons |
  | Power | square junction box | a dash-pulse (two dashes) |
  | Coolant | padded collar | one wide chevron |
  | Fuel | bolted flange | a diagonal hazard band |
  | Integrity | rivet line (three rivets) | a hairline |
  
  **Hue follows 4.2, not the icon.** A glyph is drawn in its loop hue only while that loop is *running* (emission is exposure, carried into the UI); a dead or unpowered loop's glyph is Graphite lit; a *failed* loop's glyph stays in hue because the failure is a trail, and the Alarm Red warning mark appears beside it, never over it. Icons never swap to express state. State is a reading — a needle, a fill level, a number — inside or beside the glyph. This keeps the icon set tiny (one glyph per loop, one per tool) and keeps the lie where 3.4 says it lives: in the reading, never in the frame or the glyph.
  
  **Two canonical sizes.** 16 × 16 art px (HUD, inspect view) and 24 × 24 (menus, map legend), each with a 1-art-px stroke and a 1-px inner clearance so the glyph survives on a bezel. Nothing smaller; a 12-px glyph cannot hold a flow mark.
  
  **Tool glyphs** (cutter, scanner, welder, suppressant, flare, torch, decoy) are the tool's own silhouette in profile — the same shape that breaks the crewmate's outline in 3.2 — so the hand rail teaches the in-world read. Tools are Paper White; the bound tool is Tungsten fixture.
  
  **Keybind and gamepad glyphs.** Keys are chamfered-square keycaps, Ground interior, Graphite lit border, Paper White letter in the instrument face. Gamepad face buttons are drawn the **same way** — a chamfered keycap carrying the button's letter (A/B/X/Y) — not as circles. The one grammar exception is a controller whose buttons are named by symbols rather than letters (the PlayStation set): the symbol goes inside the keycap at glyph size, accepted as a platform convention the player already owns, not a shape this UI chose. 3.4 reserves the only UI curves for dial arcs and needles, and a round button glyph would be the one closed circle on screen that is not an instrument; a keycap in the ship's dialect also lets keyboard and gamepad prompts share one component.   **Alternatives considered.** *Abstract symbols* (a drop for coolant, a flame for fuel) — rejected: they are a second vocabulary to learn and have no shape backup the player already knows. *Outlined icons with hue fill* — rejected: two colours per icon spends hue, and the outline competes with the bezel.
  
  ### 7.3 UI animation: three motions
  
  The HUD is a set of physical instruments drawn by a human hand, so it moves the way instruments move. There are exactly three motion signatures, and the player must be able to tell them apart without colour, because 2.7 already uses one of them as an honest Tell.
  
  | Signature | What it means | Motion | Rests? | Palette |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Settle** (honest change) | the ship changed; the instrument caught up | damped spring: ease-out over 250–400 ms, overshoot ≤ 5 %, then still | yes | none |
  | **Tremor** (honest stress — the Tell, 2.7) | something physical is loading the hull or the loop | ± 1 art px, irregular, 6–10 Hz, around a *true* value | returns to rest when the stress ends | none — no gleam, because nothing is lying |
  | **Glide** (the lie — class b, stage 1) | the reading has detached from the ship | smooth, uncaused drift at a slow constant rate (0.5–2 ° s⁻¹ on a dial arc), with a slow micro-wander (< 0.5 Hz) that never fully rests | **never** | violet gleam on the glass or needle edge (4.4) |
  
  **The honest/lying distinction is cause, mass and rest.** Honest motion starts with a cause the player could have seen in the world (a valve turned, a seam cracked), has mass (it eases and settles) and then rests. A tremor is honest because it is *fast, small and centred* — the shaking of a real needle on a stressed ship — and it stops when the stress stops. A glide is the one motion no real instrument makes: slow, smooth, directional, with nothing in the ship to explain it, and it never quite comes to rest. A player who learns "needles that wander are lying; needles that shake are warning" has learned Pillar 2 and Pillar 4 from the same gauge.
  
  **Digital readouts.** Honest numerals **tick** — they step once per real change and never tween. A lying readout ticks *continuously*, every few hundred milliseconds, as it tracks the glide, or holds stale while the ship audibly and visibly changes. The mechanism is always honest; only the value lies. (The audio-director decides whether a tick has a sound; the visual tick is defined here.)
  
  **What never moves.** The HUD `CanvasLayer` is **excluded from camera shake and from the hallucination presentation filter** — frame, bezels, labels and glyphs are the Corollary's anchor, and a shaking frame would teach the player that the frame can move. Readings move inside a still frame; that stillness is what makes stage-1 drift readable rather than merely unsettling (3.4).
  
  **Pulse and flash.** The Alarm Red warning mark on a failing instrument pulses **in phase with the beacon sweep** (2–3 s period, ~50 % duty), never faster — one rhythm for alarm everywhere. Nothing on the UI changes luminance faster than 3 Hz; the tremor is positional, not luminous, so it is exempt. No full-frame flashes, ever (2.8's rejected vignette).
  
  **Menus and chart table.** Cuts and short fades (80–120 ms), no slides, no bounces, no parallax. The selection bracket snaps with a 100 ms ease-out. The web map's filaments drift at ≤ 1 art px s⁻¹ in the current ring only (2.11); everything human on the map is static. Sober means almost nothing moves, and what moves is the web.
  
  **Alternatives considered.** *Sci-fi scanline/glitch for the lie* — rejected: it is a screen effect, not an instrument behaviour, and it says "the HUD is broken" when the pillar says "the gauge is wrong". *Red flashing for alarm* — rejected on photosensitivity and on 2.8. *Juicy UI (bounce, squash, scale-pop on change)* — rejected: it puts energy into the HUD, and 2.9 says sanity must never be read off the screen's energy.
  
  ### 7.4 The web map and menus
  
  **Register.** 2.11 defines the mood; this defines the furniture. Ground `#1C2128` full-bleed; one chamfered Graphite-lit border; rivet marks at the four corners only (one per corner — rivet-line detailing is a dialect cue, not a texture). Text Paper White, instrument face for labels and distances, reading face for descriptions.
  
  **Web map components.**
  
  | Element | Drawing | Note |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Depth rings | concentric steps of Ground, each ≈ 4 % darker toward centre; the inner ring's centre reaches Void Steel | the only "deeper = darker" rule carried into UI (4.6); composition pulls inward (2.11) |
  | Filaments | Hull Grey, 1 art px, branching, no right angles, density rising inward | the current ring's filaments drift; others are static |
  | Home-ship | a Tungsten fixture point with a 1-px rectilinear Foundry silhouette | the only warm mark on the chart |
  | Known wrecks | Graphite-lit rectilinear silhouettes in their donor dialect (3.3) | a visited wreck gains its dialect; an unvisited one is a plain rectangle |
  | The one visible unknown | a single 1-art-px square tick inside the wreck silhouette in Tungsten or its loop hue (no circle — 3.4), **only once seen from the pod** (2.5) | the chart records what the crew lit; it never reveals |
  | Routes | dashed rectilinear lines, Hull Grey; the planned sortie in Tungsten | human geometry over inhuman geometry (3.4) |
  | Crewmates | their beam-shape glyph (7.5) at their position | identity is beam shape, nowhere a colour |
  | Selection | Tungsten chamfered bracket around the wreck, label and distance beside it | never a filled block |

  *Designed now so the single-player HUD leaves room for it; required at VS-B, not MVP.*
  
  **The crew strip** sits top-left: one tile per crewmate, stacked. Each tile is a chamfered frame (anchor) holding:
  
  | Part | Register | Content |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Identity glyph** | anchor — the human channel (Pillar 1, 3.2) | the crewmate's beam shape (wide cone, narrow cone, split, fan) with their helmet stripe count (1–4), in Tungsten fixture |
  | **Name** | anchor | instrument face, Paper White |
  | **Voice** | anchor — the human channel is never faked | while their voice is active the identity glyph's interior fills (outline → solid) in the same Tungsten fixture; nothing else changes (the audio-director owns voice itself). *Alternative*: stepping the glyph to Tungsten beam core `#FFE2A8` reads more like "their light, brighter", but beam core is not a 4.6 UI colour; adopting it would be a 4.6 addendum (inside the Tungsten family 4.2 already permits) for the user to approve, not a quiet addition |

  | **Beam state** | reading | glyph lit = beam on, Graphite = beam off (emission is exposure, carried to the strip) |
  | **Vitals** (optional) | reading | their suit breath/warmth as needles, *if* the game-designer relays them |
