## Overview

The Synaptic Sea needs 42 systems. Its mechanical heart is a simulated life-support graph (O2, power, coolant, fuel, integrity) carried by a composite ship that the player grows by welding salvaged sections onto it; around that sit the two rhythms of the core loop (the deliberate boarding rhythm and the frantic breach rhythm), joined by an Attention system the web uses to watch the players, and a Sanity system that rewrites what the players perceive rather than how they perform. The game pillars decide the shape of the list: The World Never Lies puts the graph, trails and lighting in the foundation; Dread Before Chaos and The Web Watches make Attention and the audio tells MVP systems; Sanity Rewrites Reality isolates the Perception Filter from the simulation so a hallucination can never corrupt state; Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total adds depth rings, depletion and the failure contract at the Vertical Slice.

The tiers follow the producer-adjusted scope in the concept. **MVP** is the single-player loop test (two handmade derelicts, one weld, one Attention threshold, one horror behaviour, one hallucination class, save v1, plus a kill/continue playtest). **Vertical Slice** is split in the concept into VS-A (single-player, procedural derelicts, the shippable fallback) and VS-B (2-player LAN co-op, built only after VS-A is complete); systems marked **(VS-B)** carry the Vertical Slice tier here but must not start before VS-A. **Alpha** adds the depth rings' full content, Steam lobbies, host-owned world carry-over and accessibility settings. The template's Priority Tiers are fixed, so 'Spike phase' (weld, graph, save, lighting budget) is not a tier: it is a prototype pass over four MVP systems (Modular Ship Assembly, Life-Support Graph, Save/Load, 2D Lighting) and is listed under High-Risk Systems.

**System-by-system rationale.** Fixed-column tables cannot carry prose, so each system's scope and the reason for its tier follow here in enumeration order.

- **1. Command & Simulation Layer** (Core, MVP, inferred). Thin kernel only: fixed tick, command dispatch with authority check, a registry of state blocks owned by domain systems, change notification to presentation, and peer/authority identity on every command from day one (single-player is peer 1). Owns no domain state and defines no other system's commands. ADR-first (authority model), with a short technical spec rather than a full player-facing GDD. *Why this tier:* TD-FEASIBILITY B2: authority discipline from day one is what keeps co-op an addition rather than a rewrite. No networking in MVP; this is only the command/state separation.
- **2. Life-Support Graph** (Core, MVP, explicit). Pure-data model of O2, power, coolant, fuel and integrity loops across welded sections: node and port types, edges (seams are edges whose properties Assembly sets at weld time), flows, failure state and propagation, and per-compartment atmosphere (temperature, pressure, O2 — the P1 consequences). Separate from the scene tree so it can be serialized, tested headless and synced by summary. Stays at five loops. *Why this tier:* The core of Pillar 1; MVP hypothesis cannot be tested without it. Everything that fails, glows, leaks or is salvaged reads or writes it.
- **3. Item & Module Database** (Economy, MVP, inferred). Definitions of salvageable modules (scrubber, reactor cell, hull plate, coolant unit, data core), tools, consumables and their dialect and weights; references graph port-type IDs that the Life-Support Graph GDD defines. *Why this tier:* Salvage and welding have nothing to act on without definitions; also feeds save format.
- **4. Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera** (Core, MVP, inferred). 640x360 SubViewport world at integer scale, HUD in the root viewport, nearest filtering, snapping, Y-sort layer shape, camera. - **5. Emitter State & Light-Exposure Query** (Core, MVP, inferred). ## Game Pillars

### Pillar 1: The World Never Lies
Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only
instruments and perception can be wrong. Three channels are **inviolable** —
no hallucination may ever alter them:
- **Physical consequences.** A pipe may *look* fixed, but the room still gets
  cold, the air still thins, the pressure still drops.
- **The sane palette.** Flesh tones and violet never appear in the sane world,
  and every hallucination leaks them somewhere — a fringe, a flicker, a tint at
  the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
- **The human channel.** Voice/proximity chat and a crewmate's own light beam
  (colour and shape) are never faked. A monster that speaks in your friend's
  voice, or carries their torch, is your friend.

*Design test*: a hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe.

### Pillar 2: Dread Before Chaos
Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived
(sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress). This pillar owns tempo and
presentation; Pillar 3 owns causality.

*Design test*: breach fires at a hidden threshold vs. breach preceded by a
10–30 second escalating tell → the tell.

### Pillar 3: The Web Watches
The players' light, noise, power use and restraint raise or lower its
attention. Attention is shown in the world (creaking, flicker, filament
movement), never as a hidden meter. Depth sets the baseline; player action
moves it from there. Restraint and stealth are real strategies.

*Design test*: a flat spawn timer vs. attention-driven escalation → attention.

### Pillar 4: Sanity Rewrites Reality (and Crewmates Are Instruments)
Low sanity changes what the player perceives, not just their stats. Four
hallucination classes, each with its guard rail:
- **(a) Phantom entities.** Monsters that are not there; at depth, real ones
  hidden. A hidden real entity still leaves its P1/P2 footprint (sound, frost,
  hull stress, light disturbance) — the hallucination hides the body, never the
  trail.
- **(b) False system states.** Broken reads as fixed, fixed as broken; the lie
  extends from the gauge to the sprite. The physical consequence (P1) stays
  honest.
- **(c) Crewmates as horrors.** A teammate renders as a monster, and friendly
  harm — up to and including death — is possible. **System-gated**: harm to a
  crewmate is only possible while the *attacker's* sanity is verifiably below
  threshold, so a sane player cannot fake it. The victim sees a tell (the
  attacker's palette leak or a visible sanity sign). The game attributes the
  incident to the web — logs, scars — not to the player. Death here is like
  Project Zomboid's: it happens, and the failure contract (P5) is what makes it
  survivable for the crew.
- **(d) Phantom salvage.** A crate of treasure is garbage once it is home. At
  least one cheaper field check exists (carried weight, a second scanner, the
  palette leak); the trip home is the fallback, not the only reveal.

**No lie is unfalsifiable**: the truth is always available through the
physical world, a second instrument, a saner crewmate, the human channel, or
time — and checking costs time, risk or trust. At least one channel of truth
always remains. Solo play is supported through the first two checks; co-op adds
the human ones.

*Design test*: a hallucination that can never be disproved vs. one that costs
time, risk or trust to disprove → the costly one.
*Secondary test*: −10% move speed vs. a gauge showing a false value → the
false gauge.

### Pillar 5: Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total
Risk and reward map to depth in the web. The outer ring is kept unsafe by
depletion and wear (scrubbers degrade, salvage runs out), so there is no safe
place to farm forever. **Failure contract**: losing the home-ship or a crewmate
costs ship and body, never knowledge — decoded rules and lore persist, and the
next crew wakes knowing more.

*Design test*: safe farming vs. scarcity that pushes inward → scarcity.

**Intended tension**: Pillar 1 (legible) vs. Pillar 4 (lying). Resolved inside
the game world: the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception
are what can be wrong. The tension is the game.

> Authoring guidance: .claude/docs/templates/guidance/game-design-document-guide.md (load per-section as you author — do not read entirely).

> **Creative Director Review (CD-GDD-ALIGN)**: CONCERNS → REVISED 2026-10-26 (seven items applied: WORN descriptor mode with NONE medium; closed consequence-channel list; W_MIN_WARNING_S raised to 10 s with the exogenous-source tell requirement; duty wear W_DUTY so a fully repaired ship is never a safe harbour; closed-hatch pressure witness; header re-scoped; Game Feel re-voiced)

## Summary

The Life-Support Graph is the ship's circulation as one integer-only, scene-tree-free simulation block: five loops (O₂, power, coolant, fuel, integrity) as typed ports, nodes and edges, plus a per-compartment atmosphere (gas amount, temperature; pressure and bands derived). It is the physical ground truth every trail, gauge, hiss, breath-fog and cold-damage tick is read from, and the only thing in the game that never lies — hallucinations are tested against it, never written into it. Failures spread one hop per 10 Hz propagation run through the quantities they change, every endogenous loss is preceded by ≥ 10 s of two-channel physical warning, and welding another ship's section joins its subgraph along a seam whose sub-edges start disconnected. Everything that fails, glows, leaks or is salvaged reads or writes it through 18 published mutators and one true-value read view.

> **Quick reference** — Layer: `Core` · Priority: `MVP` · Key deps: `Command & Simulation Layer` (designed; one block `graph.state`, three hooks at divisor 6); `Ship Section & Layout Data Model` and `Item & Module Database` (undesigned — ownership and port-type contracts stated here, provisional); art bible (trail and loop grammar). Depended on by 14 systems (Failure & Trail, Suit, Emitter State, Attention, Interaction, Assembly, Horror, Perception/Instruments, Audio, Save/Load, Sanity, Web Map, Wear, Failure Contract, Co-op, Onboarding).

## Overview

The Life-Support Graph is the ship's circulation written as data: one integer-only simulation block that holds **five loops** — O₂, power, coolant, fuel and integrity — as typed ports on nodes joined by typed edges, plus one atmosphere record (gas amount, temperature) per compartment. It is the physical ground truth the whole game is measured against. Every pipe that leaks, bus that scorches, seam that frosts, scrubber that stalls and hull plate that breaches is a change to this block, made only through its published mutators inside the kernel's write scope; every gauge, trail, hiss, breath-fog and cold-damage tick is a *reading* of it. The Graph is scene-tree free, headless-testable and deterministic (same seed and command stream → identical `state_hash`), serialises as one versioned snapshot, and is the data that co-op will later sync by summary.

The player never operates the Graph as a menu or a schematic. They meet it as a place: a corridor colder than it should be, chevrons crawling slow along a pipe, mist curling from a clamp, a lamp that dims when the scrubber draws. Their verbs — patch, flip a breaker, seal a bulkhead, close a valve, vent, salvage a module, weld a section on, crank by hand — arrive as Interaction commands that call Graph mutators; welding joins another ship's subgraph to this one along a seam. Failures are physical and emergent: a starved scrubber, a frozen pipe or an overloaded cable spreads one hop per propagation run through the quantities it changes, never by script, and every endogenous loss is preceded by a readable physical warning (the fairness gate). The Graph has no notion of a hallucination: it publishes true values only, so a false "fixed" scrubber can be caught by the cold, the thinning air and the hiss the Graph still drives.

Without this system there is no Pillar 1. Without a shared, honest, falsifiable physical state, the hallucination design (Pillar 4) has nothing to lie *against*, the web has no power draw to watch (Pillar 3), and salvage and welding have nothing to act on (Pillar 5). It is the design-order-3 bottleneck with fourteen dependents, and the MVP hypothesis — *the boarding→breach loop over a visible life-support graph is tense for 30+ minutes* — cannot be tested without it.

*Implementation questions raised while designing and deferred to ADRs (→ `/architecture-decision`): struct-of-arrays packed fields vs objects (ADR-LSG-01); the fixed-point unit system (ADR-LSG-02); the explicit one-pass propagation scheme (ADR-LSG-03); append-only topology identity (ADR-LSG-04); snapshot/restore and migration (ADR-LSG-05); dirty-key encoding (ADR-LSG-06); keyed RNG (ADR-LSG-07); stable content type IDs (ADR-LSG-08); and two routed amendments outside this system — the kernel's per-block cached hash (K-1) and Save/Load's binary interchange for 64-bit values (S-1).*

## Player Fantasy

**Framing: indirect, with a direct layer on top.** The player experiences the Graph through its consequences and acts on it through physical verbs; they never see "the Graph". *(creative-director consulted; Framing A adopted with B as its competence and C as its guarantee.)*

> The ship is a body the crew assembled from other ships' corpses, and the Life-Support Graph is its circulation: oxygen, power, coolant, fuel and the hull that holds them. The player never operates the Graph as a menu. They tend the ship: a corridor colder than it should be, chevrons crawling slow along a pipe, frost fanning out from a weld seam, a hiss behind a panel. They go to it with a light and their hands, and they reroute, seal, weld or cut.
>
> Competence is literacy, not optimisation. Every failure leaves a trail along the edge it travels, thickest at its source, so a veteran crew does not run the ship better than a new one; they understand sooner what it is telling them and reach the right seam faster.
>
> And the body never lies. Gauges can be wrong and eyes can be wrong, but the cold, the thin air and the falling pressure in a compartment come from the Graph's true state for every player. When the instruments and the room disagree, the room wins, and the player learns to trust it.

**Anchor moment.** You come back up the pod tube with a salvaged scrubber on your back, and the corridor is colder than you left it. The O₂ pipe along the ceiling is still lit cyan, but its chevrons are crawling slower than they should, and there is a fine white fan of frost on the elbow by the galley. Your own breath hangs in the beam. You set the scrubber down, put your glove on the pipe, and follow the cold back to where it started — the way you would check a sleeping friend's forehead. The emotion is *caretaking under threat*: tenderness and vigilance. The power is not control; it is keeping something alive by attention — the Project Zomboid base you built with your own hands, made precarious (concept, Core Fantasy).

**Pillar alignment.** Pillar 1 verbatim: *"Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only instruments and perception can be wrong … A pipe may look fixed, but the room still gets cold, the air still thins, the pressure still drops."* The Graph is that ground truth. Pillar 2 (Dread Before Chaos): every fault has a long, readable tell before it cascades. Pillar 3: keeping the air clean draws power, and power draw is something the web can read. Pillar 4: the Graph is the falsification ground every hallucination is tested against. Pillar 5: salvage, welding and wear act on its nodes; loss is the failure contract's business, not the Graph's.

**Design test.** *When a choice makes the ship easier to read from a screen vs. easier to read from the room → choose the room. When a choice rewards running the ship well vs. rewards noticing it is unwell → choose noticing.* Corollaries: a fault persists and spreads until someone goes to it (never times out); a failure's origin is shown by a trail the player follows back along the edge, never by a marker; a hallucinated "fixed" state never quiets the real hiss or warms the real room.

**Under hallucination the fantasy deepens rather than breaks.** Pillar 4 lets the lie extend from the gauge to the sprite — a broken scrubber may render whole and spinning. What cannot change is the **consequence channel** — a closed list: compartment temperature, O₂ and pressure as the body feels them; the frost, mist, scorch and drip trails; the hiss, creak and whistle at a descriptor's anchor; lamp brightness; draught. Failure & Trail, Suit and Adaptive Audio render these as pure readers of the Graph's true values, and the Filter may neither remove nor add to them. What *can* lie is the module-body channel: sprites, gauges, inspect cards and a module's own wear state. The caretaker who can no longer trust their eyes falls back on breath, cold and touch — the oldest reading of a body. Verification costs rise in order: the room itself; a second instrument elsewhere on the ship; a saner crewmate (VS-B); time.

**Reference techniques, taken precisely.** Project Zomboid — the base degrades on its own clock and competence is the routine of noticing (*adopt*); its numeric context-menu condition readouts (*reject*). Barotrauma — repair is a place you go with the right tool; a junction box fails *where it is* (*adopt*); the Status Monitor ship-overview screen (*reject*). Dwarf Fortress fluids — propagation is visible in the medium, not announced (*adopt*). The Long Dark — cold is read from breath vapour before any number (*adopt*). SS13 / Stationeers — precision is something you go and get (*adopt* as the lit inspect card); their gas chemistry (*reject*: five loops, not chemistry). FTL — door-control causality (*adopt*); per-room O₂ shading on a schematic (*reject*). Alien: Isolation — checking costs you (*adopt*). Pandorum — the failing ship as the only reliable narrator (*adopt*).

**What this GDD does not promise (anti-pillar guard rails).**
1. No mastery-by-optimisation: no efficiency, "optimal layout", throughput score, uptime grade or any reward for running loops near capacity. Staying alive is the only payoff.
2. The web is not a puzzle to solve: failures are not authored puzzles with one correct sequence; there is no "solved" state and no completion ping.
3. No schematic, overlay, minimap or ship-status screen. Precision exists only as the lit inspect card of a specific instrument (art bible 7.0), which lies when that gauge lies. The suit's O₂ numeral on the critical strip is the *suit's* reading, not a Graph overlay.
4. No progression from the Graph: nothing unlocks or levels from repairs; better modules come from salvage.
5. No readability in the dark: "What You Light, You Can Read" — unlit compartments are readable only through the body channels (cold, breath, hiss, pressure), never by sprite state.
6. No sixth loop and no "heat loop": heat and pressure are per-compartment atmosphere.
7. No freeform plumbing: rerouting is valves, breakers, hatches, seams and cuts on pre-shaped modules.
8. No guarantee the ship can always be saved. Losing a section or the ship is allowed; the failure contract (Pillar 5) is the safety net, not the Graph.

13	- 2c: Optional Reads
14	- 2d: Present Context Summary
15	- 2e: Technical Feasibility Pre-Check
16	
17	Read all relevant context **before** asking the user anything. This is the skill's
18	primary advantage over ad-hoc design — it arrives informed.
19	
20	### 2a: Required Reads
21	
22	> **At `minimal`** (design-system is voluntary at this tier): read
23	> `design/game-brief.md` in place of the game concept, and **skip the systems-index
24	> read** — neither `game-concept.md` nor `systems-index.md` exists at `minimal`.
25	> Author from the brief's relevant MVP feature and its core loop.
26	>
27	> **This callout keys on the PROJECT tier, not this system's effective tier.**
28	> The two differ whenever `workflow_overrides.system_overrides` bumps one system
29	> above a `minimal` project — the configuration `.claude/docs/settings-guidance.md`
30	> advertises as the reason the override exists ("bump one deep system"). Those two
31	> files are absent because the *project* is `minimal`; raising *this system* to
32	> `standard` or `full` does not create them. So on a `minimal` project, take this
33	> branch **even for an overridden system**, and read the brief.
34	>
35	> The effective tier still governs everything downstream — the required section
36	> set (§1), the skeleton (§3), the section cycle (§4) and §5a. Only the
37	> required-*reads* branch here follows the project tier.
38	>
39	> **Then derive `Category`, `Layer` and `Priority` from the brief, once, here.**
40	> Six later steps are keyed on the systems index you just skipped — §2e's engine
41	> domain, Section A's and Section B's recommended options, the Visual/Audio
42	> REQUIRED table, §6 specialist routing, and §5-pre's Quick reference — and none
43	> of them has an absent-index branch. An overridden system reaches all six at
44	> `standard` or `full`, so "skip the index" leaves them with no input at all.
45	> Derive from the brief instead:
46	>
47	> - **`Category`** — one of the nine in `templates/systems-index.md`
48	>   (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio ·
49	>   Narrative · Meta`), chosen from what the brief says the system *does*.
50	> - **`Layer`** — `Foundation` if other systems depend on it, else `Feature`.
51	> - **`Priority`** — `MVP` if the brief's build order lists it, else `Post-MVP`.
52	>
53	> Carry all three for the rest of the run and treat them as the index's answer.
54	> **Mark them inferred** in §5-pre's Quick reference (*"Category: Gameplay
55	> (inferred from the brief — no systems index at this tier)"*) so a later reader
56	> does not mistake a derivation for an indexed fact. Do **not** write a systems
57	> index to hold them: `/map-systems` owns that file (§5d).

59	> Read literally without this rule, an overridden system resolves to `full`, falls
60	> through to the fail-fast reads below, and aborts with *"No game concept found.
61	> Run `/brainstorm` first"* — killing the escape hatch on step one of the very
62	> configuration it was built for.

64	- **Game concept**: Read `design/gdd/game-concept.md` — fail if missing:
65	  > "No game concept found. Run `/brainstorm` first."
66	- **Systems index**: Read `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — fail if missing:

72	  the entries this system owns and the entries that reference it:
73	  ```
74	  Grep pattern="source: design/gdd/[system-name].md" path="design/registry/entities.yaml" output_mode="content" -A 6
75	  Grep pattern="design/gdd/[system-name].md" path="design/registry/entities.yaml" output_mode="content" -B 8

78	  lines), so match the path with `-B 8` context to see the owning entry; a
79	  `referenced_by.*[system-name]` one-liner never matches it. Hold these
80	  in context as **known facts** — values that other GDDs have already
81	  established and this GDD must not contradict.

83	  Extract entries whose Domain matches this system's category. These are

147	### 2e: Technical Feasibility Pre-Check
148	
149	Before asking the user to begin designing, load engine context and surface any
150	constraints or knowledge gaps that will shape the design.
151	
152	**Step 1 — Determine the engine domain for this system:**
153	Map the system's category (from systems-index.md) to an engine domain:
154	
155	Keyed on the `Category` column of `systems-index.md`. All nine categories
156	`templates/systems-index.md` defines appear here; where a category spans several
157	engine domains, pick the row matching what the system actually does and say
158	which you picked.
159	
160	| `Category` | Engine Domain |
161	|-----------|--------------|
162	| `Gameplay` | **Physics** for combat / collision / movement; **Navigation** for AI and pathfinding; **Scripting** for rule-only systems with no engine surface |
163	| `Core` | **Core** — scene management, state, resource loading; **Input** for controls and keybinding |
164	| `UI` | UI |
165	| `Audio` | Audio |
166	| `Narrative` | Scripting — dialogue, quests, cutscenes |
167	| `Progression` | Scripting — save-adjacent rule logic, no dedicated domain |
168	| `Economy` | Scripting — data and rule logic, no dedicated domain |
169	| `Persistence` | Core — save/load, settings, serialization |
170	| `Meta` | Core — analytics, tutorials, accessibility plumbing |
171	
172	> Animation, Rendering and Networking are engine domains with no category of
173	> their own: a system needing them will be `Gameplay` or `Core`. Name the domain
174	> you read the reference for, whichever row you came in on.
175	
176	**Step 2 — Read engine context (if available):**
177	- Identify the engine and version: read `engine.name` and `engine.version` from `project.yaml`. Resolve each field independently — if its key is absent or empty (including when `project.yaml` has no `engine:` block), fall back to `.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md` (a `[TO BE CONFIGURED]` value means not set)
178	- If engine is configured, read `docs/engine-reference/[engine]/VERSION.md`
179	- Read `docs/engine-reference/[engine]/modules/[domain].md` if it exists.
180	  **If it does not exist, say so by name** — *"no engine reference for `[domain]`
181	  under `docs/engine-reference/[engine]/modules/`; feasibility not checked against
182	  the pinned engine"* — and carry that into §5-pre. A silent skip here is
183	  indistinguishable from a feasibility check that ran and found nothing wrong,
184	  which is the failure `.claude/rules/skill-authoring.md` obligation 3 exists to
185	  stop.
186	
187	  > **This is not a rare branch.** The domain table above names `Scripting` and
188	  > `Core` for five of the nine categories (`Narrative`, `Progression`, `Economy`
189	  > → Scripting; `Persistence`, `Meta` → Core), plus a sub-row each under
190	  > `Gameplay` and `Core`. The Godot reference ships `animation, audio, input,
191	  > navigation, networking, physics, rendering, ui` — **there is no
192	  > `scripting.md` and no `core.md`**. So the majority of non-`Gameplay` systems
193	  > hit the absent branch every time, and `if it exists` turned that into
194	  > silence. Either the reference gains those two files or the check reports it;
195	  > until the former, do the latter.
196	- Read `docs/engine-reference/[engine]/breaking-changes.md` for domain-relevant entries
197	- Find the domain-matching ADRs without reading every ADR to learn the field you
198	  filter on — grep the Domain field first, then read only the matches:
199	  ```
200	  Grep pattern="\*\*Domain\*\*" glob="docs/architecture/adr-*.md" output_mode="content"
201	  ```
202	  Read only the ADRs whose Domain matches this system's category (its `## Decision`
203	  and `## Engine Compatibility` sections); skip the rest.

212	Domain: [domain]

216	- [capability 2]
217

233	**Step 4 — Ask before proceeding:**

382	# /design-system — Phase 4: Section-by-Section Design
383	
384	> Part of `/design-system`. `SKILL.md` names when to read this file; the settings it
385	> resolved and the rules under its later headings still apply here.
386	
387	## 4. Section-by-Section Design
388	
389	**In this file:**
390	
391	- The Section Cycle
392	- Section-Specific Guidance
393	- Section A: Overview
394	- Section B: Player Fantasy
395	- Section C: Detailed Design (Core Rules, States, Interactions)
396	- Section D: Formulas
397	- Section E: Edge Cases
398	- Section F: Dependencies
399	- Section G: Tuning Knobs
400	- Section H: Acceptance Criteria
401	- Optional Sections: Visual/Audio, Game Feel, UI Requirements, Cross-References, Open Questions
402	
403	**Author only the sections required at the resolved tier** (§1). At `standard`,
404	the walk covers A (Overview), C (Detailed Design), E (Edge Cases),
405	F (Dependencies), H (Acceptance Criteria) — plus D (Formulas) when the system
406	defines numeric rules (see §1; the category is a hint, not the test); skip B (Player Fantasy) and
407	G (Tuning Knobs) unless `workflow_overrides.tuning_knobs: true` forces G. At
408	`full`, walk all eight (A–H). At `minimal`, the GDD is optional — if authoring
409	voluntarily, walk the standard set. Any `system_overrides.<system>` tier was
410	already folded into the resolved tier in §1.
411	
412	Walk through each required section in order. For **each section**, follow this cycle:
413	
414	### The Section Cycle
415	
416	```
417	Context  ->  Questions  ->  Options  ->  Decision  ->  Draft  ->  Approval  ->  Write
418	```
419	
420	1. **Context**: State what this section needs to contain, and surface any relevant
421	   decisions from dependency GDDs that constrain it.
422	
423	2. **Questions**: Ask clarifying questions specific to this section. Use
424	   `AskUserQuestion` for constrained questions, conversational text for open-ended
425	   exploration.
426	
427	3. **Options**: Where the section involves design choices (not just documentation),
428	   present 2-4 approaches with pros/cons. Explain reasoning in conversation text,
429	   then use `AskUserQuestion` to capture the decision.
430	
431	4. **Decision**: User picks an approach or provides custom direction.
432	
433	5. **Draft**: Write the section content in conversation text for review. Flag any
434	   provisional assumptions about undesigned dependencies.
435	
436	6. **Approval**: Per the resolved `modes.automation` mode
437	   (`.claude/docs/automation-modes.md`):
438	
439	   **In `collaborative` mode**: Immediately after the draft — in the SAME
440	   response — use `AskUserQuestion`. **NEVER use plain text. NEVER skip
441	   this step.**
442	   - Prompt: "Approve the [Section Name] section?"
443	   - Options: `[A] Approve — write it to file` / `[B] Make changes — describe what to fix` / `[C] Start over`
444	
445	   **The draft and the approval widget MUST appear together in one response.
446	   If the draft appears without the widget, the user is left at a blank prompt
447	   with no path forward — this is a protocol violation in collaborative mode.**
448	
449	   **In `guided` mode**: Write the section immediately after the draft with
450	   a brief one-line summary of what was decided. Skip the per-section widget;
451	   the multi-section authoring rule (no per-section confirmation) applies.
452	
453	   **In `autonomous` mode**: Write the section directly and call
454	   `log_decision` with `Decision point: Approve [Section Name] section`,
455	   `Chosen: [A] Approve`, `Category: minor`.
456	
457	7. **Write**: Use the Edit tool to replace the placeholder with the approved content.
458	   **CRITICAL**: Always include the section heading in the `old_string` to ensure
459	   uniqueness — never match `[To be designed]` alone, as multiple sections use the
460	   same placeholder and the Edit tool requires a unique match. Use this pattern:
461	   ```
462	   old_string: "## [Section Name]\n\n[To be designed]"
463	   new_string: "## [Section Name]\n\n[approved content]"
464	   ```
465	   Confirm the write.
466	
467	8. **Registry conflict check** (Sections C and D only — Detailed Design and Formulas):
468	   After writing, scan the section content for entity names, item names, formula
469	   names, and numeric constants that appear in the registry. For each match:
470	   - Compare the value just written against the registry entry.
471	   - If they differ: **surface the conflict immediately** before starting the next
472	     section. Do not continue silently.
473	     > "Registry conflict: [name] is registered in [source GDD] as [registry_value].
474	     > This section just wrote [new_value]. Which is correct?"
475	   - If new (not in registry): flag it as a candidate for registry registration
476	     (will be handled in Phase 5).
477	
478	After writing each section, update `production/session-state/active.md` with the
479	completed section name. Use Glob to check if the file exists — use Write to create
480	it if absent, Edit to update it if present.
481	
482	### Section-Specific Guidance
483	
484	Each section has unique design considerations and may benefit from specialist agents:
485	
486	**Every skipped spawn is announced.** When a section's review-mode check below
487	skips its specialist — in `lean` as well as `solo` — print that section's note
488	with the mode it ran in, e.g. "`creative-director` not consulted — Lean mode.
489	Review manually before production." A section drafted without its specialist
490	must say so in the output, whichever mode skipped it.
491	
492	---
493	
494	### Section A: Overview
495	
496	**Goal**: One paragraph a stranger could read and understand.
497	
498	**Derive recommended options before building the widget**: Read the system's category and layer from the systems index (already in context from Phase 2), then determine the recommended option for each tab:
499	- **Framing tab**: keyed on the `Category` column (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio · Narrative · Meta`). Player-facing — `Gameplay`, `UI`, `Audio`, `Narrative` → `[C] Both` recommended. Internal — `Core`, `Persistence`, `Meta` → `[A]` recommended. Mixed — `Economy`, `Progression` → `[C] Both`. **Tiebreak, when Layer and Category disagree** (a `Foundation`-layer `Gameplay` system is the common case): **Category wins** — the framing describes what the section is *about*, and a player-facing system stays player-facing wherever it sits in the dependency graph.
500	- **ADR ref tab**: Glob `docs/architecture/adr-*.md` and grep for the system name in the GDD Requirements section of any ADR. If a matching ADR is found → `[A] Yes — cite the ADR` recommended. If none found → `[B] No` recommended.
501	- **Fantasy tab**: Foundation/Infrastructure layer → `[B] No` recommended. All other categories → `[A] Yes` recommended.
502	
503	Append `(Recommended)` to the appropriate option text in each tab.
504	
505	**Framing questions (ask BEFORE drafting)**: Use `AskUserQuestion` with a multi-tab widget:
506	- Tab "Framing" — "How should the overview frame this system?" Options: `[A] As a data/infrastructure layer (technical framing)` / `[B] Through its player-facing effect (design framing)` / `[C] Both — describe the data layer and its player impact`
507	- Tab "ADR ref" — "Should the overview reference the existing ADR for this system?" Options: `[A] Yes — cite the ADR for implementation details` / `[B] No — keep the GDD at pure design level`
508	- Tab "Fantasy" — "Does this system have a player fantasy worth stating?" Options: `[A] Yes — players feel it directly` / `[B] No — pure infrastructure, players feel what it enables`
509	
510	Use the answers to shape the draft. **In `collaborative` mode, do NOT answer
511	these questions yourself and auto-draft** — the widget must appear. In `guided`
512	and `autonomous`, this is a MINOR framing decision: select the recommended
513	option derived above, state it in one line, and proceed (that is the whole
514	point of pre-deriving recommendations). Applies to every "ask BEFORE drafting"
515	widget in this section walk, not just this one.
516	
517	**Questions to ask**:
518	- What is this system in one sentence?
519	- How does a player interact with it? (active/passive/automatic)
520	- Why does this system exist — what would the game lose without it?
521	
522	**Cross-reference**: Check that the description aligns with how the systems index
523	describes it. Flag discrepancies.
524	
525	**Design vs. implementation boundary**: Overview questions must stay at the behavior
526	level — what the system *does*, not *how it is built*. If implementation questions
527	arise during the Overview (e.g., "Should this use an Autoload singleton or a signal
528	bus?"), note them as "→ becomes an ADR" and move on. Implementation patterns belong
529	in `/architecture-decision`, not the GDD. The GDD describes behavior; the ADR
530	describes the technical approach used to achieve it.

619	### Section D: Formulas
620	
621	**Goal**: Every mathematical formula, with variables defined, ranges specified,
622	and edge cases noted.
623	
624	**Completion Steering — always begin each formula with this exact structure:**
625	
626	```
627	The [formula_name] formula is defined as:
628	
629	`[formula_name] = [expression]`
630	
631	**Variables:**
632	| Variable | Type | Range | Source | Description |
633	|----------|------|-------|--------|-------------|
634	| [name] | float/int | [min–max] | data file / calculated / constant | [what it represents] |
635	
636	**Output Range:** [min] to [max] under normal play; [behaviour at extremes]
637	**Example:** [worked example with real numbers]
638	```
639	
640	Do NOT write `[Formula TBD]` or describe a formula in prose without the variable
641	table. A formula without defined variables cannot be implemented without guesswork.
642	
643	> **These columns must match `templates/game-design-document.md` exactly.** They
644	> did not: this block said `Symbol` where the template says `Source`, so a
645	> correctly-authored GDD was wrong against whichever of the two its reader
646	> happened to hold. `Source` is the column that stays, because it is what carries
647	> the coding-standards rule *"gameplay values must be data-driven (external
648	> config), never hardcoded"* into the design document — a variable marked
649	> `data file` is a tuning knob, one marked `constant` is a deliberate exception,
650	> and the distinction is invisible under a `Symbol` column. Put a symbol, where
651	> one helps, in the expression itself.
652	
653	**Questions to ask**:
654	- What are the core calculations this system performs?
655	- Should scaling be linear, logarithmic, or stepped?
656	- What should the output ranges be at early/mid/late game?
657	
658	**Review mode check** (apply before spawning):
659	- `solo` → skip this agent spawn. Draft the section without the specialist. Add a note: "`systems-designer` not consulted — Solo mode. Review manually before production."
660	- `lean` → skip unless this is a section with HIGH implementation risk (Sections D and H only). For other sections, draft without the agent.
661	- `full` → spawn as described below.
662	
663	**Agent delegation (MANDATORY)**: Before proposing any formulas or balance values, spawn specialist agents via `Agent` in parallel:
664	- **Always spawn `systems-designer`**: provide Core Rules from Section C, tuning goals from user, balance context from dependency GDDs. Ask them to propose formulas with variable tables and output ranges.
665	- **For economy/cost systems, also spawn `economy-designer`**: provide placement costs, upgrade cost intent, and progression goals. Ask them to validate cost curves and ratios.
666	- Present the specialists' proposals to the user for review via `AskUserQuestion`
667	- The user decides; the main session writes to file
668	- **Do NOT invent formula values or balance numbers without specialist input.** A user without balance design expertise cannot evaluate raw numbers — they need the specialists' reasoning.
669	
670	**Cross-reference**: If a dependency GDD defines a formula whose output feeds into
671	this system, reference it explicitly. Don't reinvent — connect.

675	### Section E: Edge Cases
676	
677	**Goal**: Explicitly handle unusual situations so they don't become bugs.
678	
679	**Completion Steering — format each edge case as:**
680	- **If [condition]**: [exact outcome]. [rationale if non-obvious]
681	
682	Example (adapt terminology to the game's domain):
683	- **If [resource] reaches 0 while [protective condition] is active**: hold at minimum until condition ends, then apply consequence.
684	- **If two [triggers/events] fire simultaneously**: resolve in [defined priority order]; ties use [defined tiebreak rule].
685	
686	Do NOT write vague entries like "handle appropriately" — each must name the exact
687	condition and the exact resolution. An edge case without a resolution is an open
688	design question, not a specification.
689	
690	**Questions to ask**:
691	- What happens at zero? At maximum? At out-of-range values?
692	- What happens when two rules apply at the same time?
693	- What happens if a player finds an unintended interaction? (Identify degenerate strategies)

696	- `solo` → skip this agent spawn. Draft the section without the specialist. Add a note: "`systems-designer` not consulted — Solo mode. Review manually before production."

Provide: the completed Sections C and D, and ask them to identify edge cases from the formula and rule space that the main session may have missed. For narrative systems, also spawn `narrative-director`. Present their findings and ask the user which to include.

703	defines a floor, cap, or resolution rule that this system could violate, flag it.

756	**Completion Steering — format each criterion as Given-When-Then:**
757	- **GIVEN** [initial state], **WHEN** [action or trigger], **THEN** [measurable outcome]

760	- **GIVEN** [initial state], **WHEN** [player action or system trigger], **THEN** [specific measurable outcome].
761	- **GIVEN** [a constraint is active], **WHEN** [player attempts an action], **THEN** [feedback shown and action result].
762	
763	Include at least: one criterion per core rule from Section C, and one per formula
764	from Section D. Do NOT write "the system works as designed" — every criterion must
765	be independently verifiable by a QA tester without reading the GDD.

3	
4	You are one specialist feeding the Life-Support Graph GDD for "The Synaptic Sea" (2D HD-pixel offset-top-down co-op survival-horror sim: wake in a derelict starship's cryo bay trapped in a cosmic web; repair a podcraft; salvage procedurally generated derelicts; WELD sections onto a mobile home-ship; deeper into the web = worse horrors / better loot; per-player sanity drives intense hallucinations — false system states, phantom monsters, teammates as monsters, phantom loot). Godot 4.7.2, GDScript, solo first-time dev, commercial, full rigor.
5	
6	## What the Graph is (index, authoritative)
7	"Pure-data model of O2, power, coolant, fuel and integrity loops across welded sections: node and port types, edges (seams are edges whose properties Assembly sets at weld time), flows, failure state and propagation, and per-compartment atmosphere (temperature, pressure, O2 — the P1 consequences). Separate from the scene tree so it can be serialized, tested headless and synced by summary. Stays at FIVE loops. Everything that fails, glows, leaks or is salvaged reads or writes it." Core of Pillar 1. MVP hypothesis: "the boarding->breach two-rhythm loop, over a VISIBLE life-support graph, is tense and absorbing for a 30+ minute solo session." MVP needs: visible O2/heat/power graph with propagating, physically rendered failures; one weld joining one section's nodes to the graph; save v1.
8	
9	## Pillars (must be honoured)
10	P1 The World Never Lies — pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; physical world is ground truth; only instruments/perception can be wrong. INVIOLABLE channels: physical consequences (a pipe may LOOK fixed but the room still gets cold, air thins, pressure drops), the sane palette (flesh/violet reserved for sanity), the human channel. Design test: hidden stat vs visibly leaking pipe -> the pipe.
11	P2 Dread Before Chaos. P3 The Web Watches (Attention accumulates from light, noise, POWER USE and depth; shown in the world, never a hidden meter). P4 Sanity Rewrites Reality — hallucinations are presentation-only: the simulation stays authoritative, every client receives the true value, at least one channel of truth remains; hallucinations include FALSE broken/fixed system states, which must be falsifiable by the physical world (the Graph's true values). P5 Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total.
12	Anti-pillars: not a freeform builder (welding is functional, modules pre-shaped), not a combat game, no intentional PvP, no authored story, no win.

102	## Overview
103	
104	The Synaptic Sea needs 42 systems. Its mechanical heart is a simulated life-support graph (O2, power, coolant, fuel, integrity) carried by a composite ship that the player grows by welding salvaged sections onto it; around that sit the two rhythms of the core loop (the deliberate boarding rhythm and the frantic breach rhythm), joined by an Attention system the web uses to watch the players, and a Sanity system that rewrites what the players perceive rather than how they perform. The game pillars decide the shape of the list: The World Never Lies puts the graph, trails and lighting in the foundation; Dread Before Chaos and The Web Watches make Attention and the audio tells MVP systems; Sanity Rewrites Reality isolates the Perception Filter from the simulation so a hallucination can never corrupt state; Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total adds depth rings, depletion and the failure contract at the Vertical Slice.
105	
106	The tiers follow the producer-adjusted scope in the concept. **MVP** is the single-player loop test (two handmade derelicts, one weld, one Attention threshold, one horror behaviour, one hallucination class, save v1, plus a kill/continue playtest). **Vertical Slice** is split in the concept into VS-A (single-player, procedural derelicts, the shippable fallback) and VS-B (2-player LAN co-op, built only after VS-A is complete); systems marked **(VS-B)** carry the Vertical Slice tier here but must not start before VS-A. **Alpha** adds the depth rings' full content, Steam lobbies, host-owned world carry-over and accessibility settings. The template's Priority Tiers are fixed, so 'Spike phase' (weld, graph, save, lighting budget) is not a tier: it is a prototype pass over four MVP systems (Modular Ship Assembly, Life-Support Graph, Save/Load, 2D Lighting) and is listed under High-Risk Systems.
107	
108	**System-by-system rationale.** Fixed-column tables cannot carry prose, so each system's scope and the reason for its tier follow here in enumeration order.
109	
110	- **1. Command & Simulation Layer** (Core, MVP, inferred). Thin kernel only: fixed tick, command dispatch with authority check, a registry of state blocks owned by domain systems, change notification to presentation, and peer/authority identity on every command from day one (single-player is peer 1). Owns no domain state and defines no other system's commands. ADR-first (authority model), with a short technical spec rather than a full player-facing GDD. *Why this tier:* TD-FEASIBILITY B2: authority discipline from day one is what keeps co-op an addition rather than a rewrite. No networking in MVP; this is only the command/state separation.
111	- **2. Life-Support Graph** (Core, MVP, explicit). Pure-data model of O2, power, coolant, fuel and integrity loops across welded sections: node and port types, edges (seams are edges whose properties Assembly sets at weld time), flows, failure state and propagation, and per-compartment atmosphere (temperature, pressure, O2 — the P1 consequences). Separate from the scene tree so it can be serialized, tested headless and synced by summary. Stays at five loops. *Why this tier:* The core of Pillar 1; MVP hypothesis cannot be tested without it. Everything that fails, glows, leaks or is salvaged reads or writes it.
112	- **3. Item & Module Database** (Economy, MVP, inferred). Definitions of salvageable modules (scrubber, reactor cell, hull plate, coolant unit, data core), tools, consumables and their dialect and weights; references graph port-type IDs that the Life-Support Graph GDD defines. *Why this tier:* Salvage and welding have nothing to act on without definitions; also feeds save format.
113	- **4. Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera** (Core, MVP, inferred). 640x360 SubViewport world at integer scale, HUD in the root viewport, nearest filtering, snapping, Y-sort layer shape, camera. Art bible 8.1/8.4. *Why this tier:* Every visual system sits on it; the lighting spike (8.12) starts here.
114	- **5. Emitter State & Light-Exposure Query** (Core, MVP, inferred). Simulation-side record of every light emitter (fixtures, beams on/off and cone shape, machinery-node lanterns, deployables, power draw), written through commands, plus a geometric light-exposure query (cone test and occluder raycasts on physics shapes) that Attention, Horror Entities and Interaction use. Runs headless; never reads Light2D. *Why this tier:* TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY: keeps light a simulation input no hallucination can touch, and lets Attention run headless and on the host for remote players.
115	- **6. 2D Lighting & Occlusion** (Core, MVP, explicit). Rendering only: reads emitter state and draws Light2D, occluders, ambient floors, the material-level hull floor, the six shadow-casting slots, emission glow and light textures. Owns the final Light2D values through a modifier contract: Attention flicker, horror light disturbance and Perception Filter decoys submit layered modifiers; the Filter may add decoy visuals but never changes the real reveal radius (a pillar anchor). *Why this tier:* Identity-defining and the art bible's first spike: if lighting does not fit the frame budget the whole direction needs a trade-off.
116	- **7. Player Controller & Input** (Core, MVP, inferred). Movement, 5-facing sprite with mirrored facings, per-facing chest point for the beam (user decision 2026-10-26: chest-mounted lamp), gamepad/keyboard input mapping, stiff-weighted animation states. *Why this tier:* Nothing is playable without a body to light.
117	- **8. Interaction System** (Gameplay, MVP, inferred). Inspect, cut, weld, open, carry, run a field check; the act-only-on-lit rule uses the light-exposure query (prompts drawn only for lit objects is the UI side, 7.0); hold-to-confirm on destructive actions; proximity focus for gamepad. Falsification checks reach Sanity as commands from here. Also owns the friendly-harm act: tool use against a crewmate is an Interaction command accepted only when Sanity's gate reports the actor below threshold (no dedicated damage or combat system — Anti-Pillar), with no reward path. *Why this tier:* The verb layer for boarding; encodes the 'spend light to act' rule.
118	- **9. Failure & Trail System** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Pure reader: maps graph failure state and footprint sources to physical trail visuals (frost, mist, scorch, drip, hairlines) in the three sizes, writing only CanvasItem/Material/particles. Owns no propagation and no atmosphere — both are Graph state. Tagged as a truth channel: immune to the Perception Filter. *Why this tier:* Pillar 1 made visible; the honest channel every hallucination is checked against.
119	- **10. Suit & Equipment** (Gameplay, MVP, inferred). Suit vitals (O2, integrity, local temperature and pressure read from the Graph's compartment atmosphere) as a PER_PLAYER block keyed by PlayerId, loadout and tool slots, the chest-mounted lamp (hands-free; the four beam shapes) and deployables — including throwable glowsticks (user decision 2026-10-26) — as emitters, carried modules. Each tool's effect is defined by the system it acts on (cutter/welder: Interaction and Assembly; scanner: Sanity falsification; suppressant: Attention/Horror). *Why this tier:* Personal survival state and the beam are the player's two instruments; the suit layer HUD reads from here.
120	- **11. Ship Section & Layout Data Model** (Core, MVP, inferred). The runtime section schema shared by authoring, procgen, assembly and save: tile layer reference, collision shapes, sockets, seams, graph-node references, salvage/module slots, and the pure-data ship layout (sections, transforms, welds) that is projected onto the scene tree. *Why this tier:* TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY: without a single owner three GDDs would each define a socket; needed before the weld spike.
121	- **12. Ship Body & Interior Physics** (Core, MVP, inferred). The composite ship as one physics body with a ship-local reference frame; characters and props moving inside a moving body (the moving-platform problem); detach spawns a new body. *Why this tier:* TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY: the spike is weld-on-a-moving-ship and nothing owned the motion; needed before the weld spike.
122	- **13. Modular Ship Assembly** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Weld and cut sections as atomic one-tick commands across graph join and layout change: join validation is a pure Graph query; seams set edge properties; cap plates; detach into a new body. Also owns module install/uninstall (cut a scrubber free, install it at home) as a graph mutation distinct from section welding. *Why this tier:* The game's hook and its riskiest build task (producer: the weld is the hardest MVP item); first spike.
123	- **14. Derelict Authoring (Handmade Kits)** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Hand-built Foundry-dialect derelict and spawn ship from the room kit (6.3): tagged sockets, graph nodes, salvage slots, one visible unknown per wreck. *Why this tier:* MVP uses two handmade derelicts; the kit definition is also what procgen later assembles.
124	- **15. Boarding & Salvage** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). The boarding rhythm: enter, listen, light, decide, cut a module free, carry it home under rising Attention; field checks for suspect salvage. *Why this tier:* The 5-minute loop. Without it there is no sortie.
125	- **16. Web Map & Transit** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). The web world model (derelict list, seeds plus deltas, what is loaded) and the abstracted pod hop between home-ship and target (state 2.5), docking, fuel cost. Full flight is out of scope. Depth Rings extends it at VS; the Chart Table only displays it. *Why this tier:* Connects the two ends of the MVP sortie at minimum cost.
126	- **17. Attention System** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). The web's attention. Owns a stimulus-input API (light via the exposure query; noise and power stimuli pushed in by Graph, Suit, Interaction, Assembly and Horrors — never read from Audio), baseline set by depth, and the BREACH STATE MACHINE (calm → tell window → breach → subsiding). Owns the tell-window contract — every breach is preceded by a 10–30 s escalating tell the player could perceive — which Horror Entities, Graph failure injection, Lighting modifiers and Audio must all honour; the contract is a testable acceptance criterion written before Horror and Audio are designed. Its presentation (filaments in the light cone, creaks, flicker as a Lighting modifier) reads attention level plus emitter state. Pillars 2 and 3. *Why this tier:* The hinge between the two rhythms; core hypothesis cannot be tested without it.
127	- **18. Horror Entities** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Segment-rig horrors with creep/unfold/snap behaviours, real occlusion and shadow; writes hidden-entity footprints (branching rime, radial hairlines, light disturbance) into the Graph footprint channel and submits light-disturbance modifiers to Lighting. MVP: one behaviour. *Why this tier:* Gives Attention consequences; MVP minimum is one behaviour.
128	- **19. Sanity & Hallucination Rules** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Per-player sanity, its drift order, the four hallucination classes and their guard rails (inviolable channels, no unfalsifiable lie, system-gated friendly harm, verification cost). Authoritative; writes per-player perception state keyed by a stable PlayerId (seat), never by transport peer ID, from MVP; receives falsification checks as commands from Interaction/Suit. No simulation system ever reads perception state — the friendly-harm gate reads the sanity level, not perception. *Why this tier:* Pillar 4 and the hook. MVP: class (b) false system state only.
129	- **20. Perception Filter** (Gameplay, MVP, explicit). Per-client perceived-value query/decorator service (displayed value of X for local peer P) plus screen-wide effects: stage-1/2/3 drift, the violet fringe, palette leak, Light2D decoy modifiers. Owns no instrument or HUD nodes — Instruments and HUD ask it and draw the result. Defines the truth-channel/corruptible tag contract on presentation nodes (trails, true reveal radius, crewmate beams, character sprites, HUD frame immune; gauges and machine sprites corruptible). Owns the class-(c) victim tell as a truth-channel element: the below-threshold crewmate's violet fringe with mandatory breathing and the P1 proximity cue (art bible 5.5), rendered for every saner viewer and attributed to the web in logs and scars. Reads simulation state, writes only CanvasItem/Material/Light2D. *Why this tier:* Isolating it keeps hallucinations from touching the simulation (TD rule) and gives the debug overlay something to contrast.
130	- **21. HUD & Suit Layer** (UI, MVP, explicit). Centre-bottom critical strip, bottom-left suit panel, hand rail, warning mark, tri-modal lying-reading signatures, HR-1..15. *Why this tier:* How the player reads their own body; Section 7 of the art bible specifies it.
131	- **22. In-World Instruments & Inspect View** (UI, MVP, explicit). Owns the gauge, sight-glass and dial nodes as lit sprites and the inspect view (the same instrument magnified); asks the Perception Filter for the displayed value and draws it with the settle/tremor/glide motion signatures. *Why this tier:* Where class (b) lies live; pairs with the Failure & Trail System as the truth check.
132	- **23. Chart Table (Web Map & Menus)** (UI, MVP, explicit). The never-lying human instrument: web map, route planning, pause panel, menus. MVP: pick a target, pause, save. *Why this tier:* Needed to start a sortie; the web map grows in later tiers.
133	- **24. Adaptive Audio & Tells** (Audio, MVP, explicit). Distinct running and failing sound per loop read directly from Graph state (so audio tells can lead visuals), horror and Attention cues, the P1 proximity cue. Must state whether audio can lie: if it can, audio corruption joins the Perception Filter's write set under the same rule; the voice channel is never faked either way. Audio is the only non-visual Attention channel. *Why this tier:* Pillar 2 and the accessibility consequence of 'no Attention indicator': sound carries the weight.
134	- **25. Save/Load & Versioned Format** (Persistence, MVP, explicit). A versioned state-block registration contract: each domain system registers its serializable state block through the Command kernel's registry, and Save/Load serializes and migrates the set (format version from v1; host-owned). Domain systems depend on this contract, not the reverse. Also owns the MVP death stub: on crew death the game reloads the last save (placeholder, replaced by Failure Contract & Re-wake at VS-A) so no MVP GDD improvises its own. *Why this tier:* A no-win-state game that breaks saves on every module change cannot be played long; versioning is cheapest on day one.
135	- **26. Debug Overlay (True Values)** (Meta, MVP, inferred). Developer-only overlay showing authoritative values beside the hallucinated ones, to tell deliberate corruption from real desync. Never exposed as an accessibility feature (R-7). *Why this tier:* TD-FEASIBILITY: needed from the start; also the QA instrument for the sanity system.
136	- **27. Procedural Derelict Generation** (Gameplay, Vertical Slice, explicit). Seeded generator assembling hand-authored kit chunks by grammar: continuity, one trail per source, hero cap, clear path (6.3 rules), salvage placement, one visible unknown. Host sends seed plus deltas. *Why this tier:* VS-A: the point where it becomes a repeatable game rather than a prototype; deliberately after the loop is proven.
137	- **28. Depth Rings & Scarcity** (Progression, Vertical Slice, explicit). Rings of the web: Attention baseline, ambient and iridescence per ring, salvage value, horror roster. Pillar 5. VS: one ring beyond the spawn ring. Ring access in VS-A is gated by ship capability (pod range, life-support margin) read from the Graph and Assembly, so the shipped fallback has an implicit capability ladder; Ship Capability Progression formalises it at Alpha. *Why this tier:* Gives 'deeper is richer' a mechanism.
138	- **29. Resource Depletion & Wear** (Economy, Vertical Slice, explicit). Scrubbers and plates degrade; outer-ring salvage runs out, so there is no safe place to farm forever. *Why this tier:* The enforcement mechanism for Pillar 5 the creative-director asked for.
139	- **30. Knowledge Codex & Logs** (Progression, Vertical Slice, explicit). Decoded web rules, horror tells and recovered logs that persist across crew loss; some rules shift with depth so the web never becomes solvable. Knowledge must change play, not just be stored: a decoded tell becomes recognisable earlier, a learned rule is annotated on the Chart Table, and a recovered log names a deeper wreck on the Web Map (the session hook). Acceptance criterion: every codex entry has a stated effect on play. *Why this tier:* The currency of the failure contract and the Discovery aesthetic.
140	- **31. Failure Contract & Re-wake** (Progression, Vertical Slice, explicit). Losing the ship or a body costs ship and body, never knowledge; the next crew wakes in the cryo bay knowing more (state 2.10). Owns the cryo-bay fiction as a throughline: re-wake presents the mystery (pod count, pod states, what changes each wake, who else is in the pods and why they keep waking), co-authored with narrative-director, with lore fragments fed through the Knowledge Codex. Includes lethal friendly harm's consequences. The GDD's Player Fantasy section opens with the cryo bay, not a respawn rule. *Why this tier:* Pillar 5's contract; prevents the death spiral.
141	- **32. Environmental Storytelling Placement** (Narrative, Vertical Slice, explicit). The cause/verb/absence three-sentence verdict per wreck, placed by tagged slots; no bodies, only empty suits. *Why this tier:* Delivers lore without text or cutscenes; makes procgen derelicts read as places.
142	- **33. Co-op Session & Replication (VS-B)** (Core, Vertical Slice, explicit). Listen-server host-authoritative 2-player LAN: spawner/synchronizers, request validation, summary-state sync of the graph. Built only after VS-A is complete. *Why this tier:* VS-B; gated behind the single-player slice per TD-FEASIBILITY.
143	- **34. Chat, Voice & Pings (VS-B)** (Core, Vertical Slice, explicit). Voice/proximity, text chat and world pings: the human channel, never hallucinated, with a speaker indicator. *Why this tier:* The costly-check channel Pillar 4 relies on; deaf/HoH and no-mic crews need text and pings.
144	- **35. Crew Strip HUD (VS-B)** (UI, Vertical Slice, explicit). Identity glyph (beam shape plus stripe count), name, voice activity, location, beam state; no sanity, no vitals, no locators. *Why this tier:* Co-op readability without breaking the human-channel rule.
145	- **36. Onboarding (Cryo Bay)** (Meta, Vertical Slice, explicit). The first ten minutes: one sealed bay, one failing loop, follow the trail, fix it, watch the gauge agree. Teaches the boarding rhythm and the first Attention threshold. *Why this tier:* A slow-start game dies without it; MVP playtesters get a hand-led version.
146	- **37. Sanity Scars & Character History** (Progression, Alpha, explicit). Permanent suit-repair-style scars in three slots; how earned, how many, whether guests keep them (open question). *Why this tier:* Gives sanity lasting weight; depends on the failure contract and the guest-carry-over decision.
147	- **38. Ship Capability Progression** (Progression, Alpha, explicit). Life-support margin, range, hull as the ladder players climb as they graft. *Why this tier:* The Achiever ladder; not needed to test the loop.
148	- **39. Steam Lobby & NAT** (Core, Alpha, explicit). Steam lobbies and NAT traversal so friends connect over the internet. Needs a technology evaluation first. *Why this tier:* A separate milestone from LAN co-op (TD).
149	- **40. Host-Owned World & Guest Carry-over** (Persistence, Alpha, explicit). Whose save owns the shared ship; what guests keep; copying a save to let a guest host. Open design question for game-designer and creative-director. *Why this tier:* B1 decision made structural: no live host migration.
150	- **41. Accessibility Settings** (Meta, Alpha, explicit). UI scale, reading-face scale, HUD opacity floor, reduced motion preserving the backbone, bounded low-vision ambient floor, pattern strength, captions policy (R-6). *Why this tier:* Design starts early because several settings change what other systems must expose.
151	- **42. Settings & Input Rebinding** (Meta, Alpha, inferred). Graphics, audio, controls, key and button rebinding, gamepad completeness enumeration (HR-14). *Why this tier:* Expected on PC; not needed to test the loop.

153	**Relationship analysis.** The heaviest dependency roots are listed in the data line below; they are the project's bottlenecks. Command & Simulation Layer sits under almost everything because TD-FEASIBILITY made 'every mutation is an authority-checked request' the rule that keeps co-op additive. The Life-Support Graph is the data every visible system reads. The Item & Module Database is a quiet bottleneck: salvage, welding, save format, depletion and depth rings all need its definitions, so it should be designed early despite looking like content. Lighting is both a Foundation-adjacent technical risk and the carrier of three pillars. The Perception Filter is deliberately a query service with many readers and no simulation writers: it is the isolation that makes Sanity safe. The Emitter State & Light-Exposure Query exists for the mirror-image reason: light must stay a simulation input the Filter cannot touch. UI and Audio systems depend on gameplay systems, never the reverse, so they can be designed after the rules they display.

222	## Circular Dependencies
223	
224	- **None found** in the hard dependency graph (checked programmatically at generation: every system resolves to a finite depth).
225	- *Soft cycle — Attention <-> Lighting.* Light raises Attention, and Attention makes web filaments visible in the light cone. Resolution: one-way data flow. Lighting exposes an emitter registry; Attention reads it and publishes an attention level; the filament renderer (part of Attention's presentation) reads both. Lighting never reads Attention.
226	- *Soft cycle — Sanity <-> Perception Filter.* Sanity decides what is perceived; the Filter draws it. Resolution: Sanity is authoritative and writes only perception state; the Filter reads that state and writes only CanvasItem/Material/Light2D properties (control-manifest rule from TD-FEASIBILITY). The Filter never calls back.
227	- *Soft cycle — Life-Support Graph <-> Modular Ship Assembly.* Assembly changes the graph's shape; the graph decides what assembly may join. Resolution: the graph is pure data; Assembly mutates it only through the Command layer.

=== concept MVP ===
## MVP Definition

**Core hypothesis**: The boarding→breach two-rhythm loop, over a visible
life-support graph, is tense and absorbing for a 30+ minute solo session.

**Required for MVP** (single-player):
1. One handmade spawn derelict and one handmade target derelict, with an
   abstracted pod hop between them.
2. Visible O₂ / heat / power graph with propagating, physically rendered
   failures.
3. One weld: attach one section and join its nodes to the graph.
4. Attention with one threshold and one horror behaviour.
5. Sanity as a single hallucination class (false system state), falsifiable by
   the physical world.
6. Save/load v1 with a format version.
7. All state changes through a single command/simulation layer (no networking
   code, no replication).

**Explicitly NOT in MVP**: procedural generation, co-op, multiple horrors,
other hallucination classes, lore, Steam, art at final fidelity, adaptive
audio.

**Kill/continue gate at the end of MVP**: playtest with at least three people
outside the project. If a 30+ minute solo session is not tense and absorbing,
iterate on the loop before any VS-A work. No procgen on an unproven loop.

### Scope Tiers (if budget/time shrinks)

| Tier | Content | Features | Timeline (solo; low confidence until spikes produce velocity) |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Spike phase** | Throwaway prototypes | Weld on a moving ship (tilemap + collision + graph merge); graph with spreading failures; save round-trip with version; 2D lighting budget on D3D12 | 4–8 weeks |
| **MVP** | 2 handmade derelicts | Core loop only (list above) + playtest gate | 6–9 months full-time / 10–16 part-time |
| **VS-A** (single-player, **the shippable fallback**) | Outer ring of the web map; one procgen room kit | Procgen derelicts; 2nd horror type; all 4 hallucination classes with falsification checks; one derelict kit at target HD-pixel fidelity under the lighting model | +8–12 months |
| **VS-B** (co-op) | Same content | 2-player LAN listen-server; authority model proven with two local instances | +4–6 months, only after VS-A is complete |
| **Alpha** | 3 depth rings; full kit set; lore fragments | Steam lobbies / NAT; crew scars and knowledge persistence (failure contract); versioned saves; host-owned world + guest carry-over; true-value debug overlay | +12–18 months |
| **Full Vision** | Early Access launch | Polish; adaptive audio; accessibility; onboarding | ~4–6 years total |

**What ships if time runs out**: VS-A, as a small single-player survival-horror
game. Co-op and depth rings are cut; the product is whole.

const NAME2SLUG = {}
for (const s of SYSTEMS) NAME2SLUG[s.name] = s.slug
const pathOf = (name) => DESIGNED[name] || ('design/gdd/' + NAME2SLUG[name] + '.md')

// dependency depth (in-workflow deps only) for a safe topological start order
const depth = {}
function depthOf(s) {
  if (depth[s.slug] != null) return depth[s.slug]
  let d = 0
  for (const n of s.deps) if (NAME2SLUG[n]) d = Math.max(d, 1 + depthOf(SYSTEMS.find(x => x.name === n)))
  depth[s.slug] = d
  return d
}
SYSTEMS.forEach(depthOf)
SYSTEMS.sort((a, b) => (depth[a.slug] - depth[b.slug]) || (a.order - b.order))

function sysBlock(s, depStatus) {
  const deps = s.deps.map(n => `  - ${n} -> ${pathOf(n)} [${depStatus[n]}]`).join('\n')
  const dependents = SYSTEMS.filter(x => x.deps.includes(s.name)).map(x => x.name)
  return `SYSTEM: ${s.name} (index row ${s.order}; Category ${s.cat}; Layer ${s.layer}; Priority MVP). GDD path: design/gdd/${s.slug}.md. Stage dir: ${SCR}/${s.slug} (call it <SCR>).
Specialist routing (design-system Section 6, from the index Recommended Design Order): primary ${s.primary}; supporting ${s.support.join(', ')}.
Required extras by category: Visual/Audio ${['Gameplay', 'UI', 'Audio', 'Narrative'].includes(s.cat) ? 'REQUIRED (art-director consulted)' : 'optional (write a real note, not a placeholder)'}; Game Feel ${['Gameplay', 'UI'].includes(s.cat) ? 'REQUIRED' : 'optional (write a real note)'}; Cross-References REQUIRED; UI Requirements and Open Questions always written.
Upstream dependencies (status at the moment this stage started):
${deps}
Downstream dependents among the systems being designed in this run: ${dependents.length ? dependents.join('; ') : 'none in this run'}.
ROUTED THREADS this GDD must carry (decisions already made elsewhere; honour verbatim): ${s.threads}`
}

const REVIEW_S = { type: 'object', properties: { verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['PASS', 'REVISE'] }, items: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { section: { type: 'string' }, severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['blocking', 'major', 'minor'] }, problem: { type: 'string' }, fix: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['section', 'severity', 'problem', 'fix'] } }, registry_conflicts: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } }, size_kb: { type: 'number' } }, required: ['verdict', 'items', 'registry_conflicts', 'size_kb'] }

// ---- helpers ----
const SON = { model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
async function tryAgent(prompt, opts, tries) {
  for (let i = 0; i < (tries || 2); i++) {
    const r = await agent(i === 0 ? prompt : prompt + '\n\n(RETRY ' + i + ': a previous attempt died; resume from whatever already exists on disk — do not redo finished work.)', opts)
    if (r) return r
  }
  return null
}
let regChain = Promise.resolve()
function serial(fn) { const p = regChain.then(fn, fn); regChain = p.catch(() => {}); return p }

const doneP = {}, resolveDone = {}
for (const s of SYSTEMS) doneP[s.slug] = new Promise(res => { resolveDone[s.slug] = res })
const results = {}

async function runSystem(s) {
  const L = (stage) => ({ label: `${stage}:${s.slug}` })
  const out = { slug: s.slug, name: s.name, status: 'failed', stages: {} }
  try {
    // 0. wait for in-run dependencies
    const depStatus = {}
    for (const n of s.deps) {
      if (DESIGNED[n]) { depStatus[n] = 'designed' ; continue }
      const r = await doneP[NAME2SLUG[n]]
      depStatus[n] = r && r.status === 'done' ? 'designed in this run' : 'FAILED in this run — treat as undesigned; state a provisional contract'
    }
    log(`▶ ${s.name}: dependencies settled, starting brief`)
    const SB = sysBlock(s, depStatus)

    // 1. Brief
    const brief = await tryAgent(`${COMMON}\n\n${SB}\n\nSTAGE 1 — CONTEXT BRIEF (design-system Phase 2, all of 2a-2e). Produce <SCR>/brief.md, the single context document every later stage of this system reads. Do the reads: the index row + rationale bullet + dependency-map entries for this system; the concept pillars, core loop and MVP definition; the registry entries this GDD will own or read (grep every constant/formula whose referenced_by names design/gdd/${s.slug}.md, and every "# pending referenced_by" comment naming it); for EVERY upstream GDD that exists, its Interactions-with-Other-Systems row and its Dependencies / Formulas / Edge Cases / Tuning Knobs / Cross-References sections where they mention this system by name (grep the system name and its obvious short forms, e.g. "Suit", "Attention", "Filter"), quoting the exact contract text with file:line; the Graph GDD's Interactions row and Cross-References for this system even if it is not a direct dependency (it names most MVP systems); the art bible sections that govern this system; the reflexion log entries whose Domain touches this category; the engine reference for this system's domain (VERSION.md + breaking-changes.md; name the modules file or say none exists). Write brief.md with these headings: Mandate (index wording verbatim + why this tier), Pillar mapping (primary / serves, with the design tests), Locked facts (table: fact, value, owner file:line — registry + dependency GDDs), Contracts expected of this system by its dependents (quoted, file:line), Provisional contracts for undesigned or in-flight dependencies, Routed threads (restate each thread and where it lands in the GDD), Past failure patterns (reflexion), Engine feasibility brief (capabilities / constraints / knowledge gaps marked HIGH/MEDIUM / ADRs: none exist yet), Open design decisions (each: point, 2-4 options with pros/cons, recommended option, reason — these are the decisions the Section Cycle would have asked the user), Risks, Scope guard (what this GDD must NOT absorb from neighbours). Be concrete: names, numbers, ids. Return the schema fields; file is the brief path.`, { ...SON, phase: 'Brief', schema: BRIEF_S, ...L('brief') })
    if (!brief) throw new Error('brief failed')

    // 2. Rulings (advisor, session model)
    const rulings = await agent(`${COMMON}\n\n${SB}\n\nSTAGE 2 — ADVISOR RULINGS. You are the design advisor (the stronger model) standing in for the orchestrator who, in the single-session /design-system run, made numbered rulings that bound every specialist (precedent: the Graph GDD's 24 rulings). Read <SCR>/brief.md fully. For each open decision in it, rule: pick the option, say why in one or two sentences, name the pillar or locked fact that decides it. State the GDD rule-id prefix to use (2-3 letters, e.g. SL-, IDB-, EM-) and the section-size bar: docs.density thorough, the kernel and Graph GDDs are the bar (numbered rules with names, tables for states and interfaces, every formula with the lead-in + variable table + output range + worked example, 25+ edge cases as If/then, 30+ tuning knobs, 40+ GWT acceptance criteria with (auto)/(lint)/(review)/(manual)/(spike) tags). Return the schema (file, two-sentence summary, flags = conflicts/risks).`

Every locked constant/formula name is used VERBATIM with its registry value. Prefix every rule with the id prefix the rulings set. Log one decision per section approval and one per framing/approach choice (LOGGING). Density: thorough — the kernel and Graph GDDs are the bar; a thin section is bounced by the reviewer.     let a1 = await tryAgent(`${COMMON}\n\n${SB}\n\nSTAGE 4a — AUTHOR, PART 1. Read <SCR>/brief.md, <SCR>/rulings.md and the specialist files. ${AUTH_RULES}\nWrite, in order: ## Overview (framing: ${['Core', 'Persistence', 'Meta'].includes(s.cat) ? 'data/infrastructure layer with its player impact' : 'both the data layer and its player-facing effect'}; what it is in one sentence, how the player meets it, what the game loses without it; index wording reconciled); ## Player Fantasy (from the creative-director proposal: framing, anchor moment, pillar quote, design test, under-hallucination paragraph, reference techniques adopt/reject, anti-pillar guard rails); ## Detailed Design with ### Core Rules (numbered, named), ### States and Transitions (table: state, entry, exit, transitions, who may cause them), ### Interactions with Other Systems (table per upstream and downstream system: data in, data out, interface owner, exact hook/mutator/read_view/dirty-key names where fixed elsewhere; bidirectional consistency with the dependency GDD's own Interactions row — quote it); ## Dependencies (table: system, direction, hard/soft, interface, status designed/in-flight/undesigned-provisional); ## Cross-References (table: this GDD's reference -> other GDD section/registry name).
